articles.title: This year's best Black Friday laptop deals in the US and UK — our top picks from Dell, Amazon, Best Buy, HP, Lenovo, Currys, and more
articles.content: With component prices soaring and discounts getting smaller, I'm expecting it'll be a lot harder to find some truly exceptional Black Friday laptop deals this year. But signs from some of the early sales are positive, with several strong offers that are worth considering if you're planning to buy a new device in the end-of-year sales. You can find all of the best ones right here. It's still a little quieter in the US, as we're waiting for some of the big names to kick off sales. However, both Best Buy and Dell are already serving up some big savings on laptops at this early stage, and are the places to go if you're shopping right now. It's a lot busier in the UK, where the likes of Currys, Argos, Samsung, and Dell have all already launched Black Friday sales. It's here that you can find some good savings on mid-range and high-end devices, including some powerful and modern laptops from Acer, Microsoft, Lenovo, and more. But this is very much just the start, and I expect many more Black Friday laptop deals will drop over the coming weeks. It may be a tougher year to find the exceptional bargains, but we'll bring all the best ones we can find to you right here. Getting a 512GB SSD in a laptop of this price is a bit of a steal, though, when you usually see only 256GB at a maximum. That's a nice bonus if you have lots of files, photos or videos you want to store. It also has a more modern processor, which isn't dramatically more powerful, but will be better supported and more efficient for general use. articles.title: AWS had its agents build a free and open emulator for AWS. They now maintain it, too.
articles.content: AWS on Wednesday launched an emulator for AWS called AWS Emulator. That, by itself, is interesting and may raise some questions about the future of LocalStack . But what’s maybe most interesting is that the emulator was entirely built by a team of agents and will also be maintained by them going forward. Since AWS wasn’t sure it could actually copyright the work of these agents — and didn’t want to assert copyright where none may exist — the emulator is available under the Creative Commons Zero license , which puts the code into the public domain. Tom ‘Spot’ Callaway, a principal open source software strategist at AWS, told The New Stack that there have obviously been other emulators in the past — and AWS itself has built some, too. “The challenge is that they get out of date very quickly,” he explains. “They don’t always reflect reality on the ground, and because of that, they’re often not trusted. And we didn’t even trust them internally.” With the rise of agentic coding tools , the team also saw a need for a better emulator that could help agents test code against AWS services without having to hand over AWS credentials to the agents. The agent system building AWS Emulator. Credit: AWS. Meanwhile, the team was also looking at a test case for building a full project with agents, and the emulator proved to be a good testing ground, in large part because it provided a bounded problem with clear goals and the ability to test the results. Since AWS already publishes a full set of API models as Smithy models and generates all its SDKs from those files, “there’s no reason that we can’t also generate mock emulation around that same logic,” Callaway says. A weekend Kiro experiment The project goes back to an experiment by Matt Goldberg, a senior principal engineer on the AWS Developer Tools team. Callaway says the team was “heavily inspired by the Anthropic work where they instantiated a compiler,” referring to the C compiler that Anthropic researchers had a team of agents build earlier this year. Goldberg writes in a blog post that he first asked Kiro , AWS’s agentic coding tool, to build an emulator for Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS). It came back with a first version 15 minutes later. He then had Kiro build out the rest of AWS over a weekend. That version unsurprisingly had gaps, he notes, but his team started testing its own software against it the following Monday. “I got to admit, the first time I heard about this, I was like, ‘Are we sure this is a good idea?’” Callaway says. The more the team iterated on it, he adds, the more comfortable he became that this was a good problem for agents to take on. In its current version, AWS Emulator supports 438 public AWS API models covering more than 200 services. As AWS updates them and releases new services, the agents will quickly update the emulator, too. Callaway expects the gap between a new AWS service launching and the emulator supporting it to be “days, not weeks, not months,” though he notes the team hasn’t yet seen how that plays out with the project in public. The emulator itself is written in Rust and runs locally on Linux, macOS, and Windows, without a network connection or an AWS account. “There’s no AI inside of AWS Emulator,” Callaway says. “It does not do an LLM callout at all.” Three teams of agents AWS says it divides the work among three teams of agents. The first develops test scenarios from the public Smithy models and runs them against real AWS services to establish how the emulator should behave. These scenarios can involve several services working together, rather than just individual API calls. As Callaway explains, “if the docs don’t tell the truth, then the cloud becomes the source of truth.” The second team runs those scenarios against…

articles.title: Elon Musk's Grok Build coding agent is leaking a serious amount of confidential data
articles.content: Researchers found Grok Build apps were widely exposed due to insecure default sharing settings and discoverable URLs Thousands of accessible apps leaked sensitive business data, healthcare records, passwords, and internal documents SpaceXSI remediated the issue after disclosure, highlighting security risks in AI-generated application platforms Grok Build, an AI-powered coding agent built by Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI, has been found leaking a mind-numbing amount of confidential data, thanks to an apparent misconfiguration in how the products are being published on the platform. SpaceXSI, established when SpaceX and xAI merged , has a product called Grok Build, which allows users to create web applications by simply describing what they want in a chatlike interface. Without having to write any of the code themselves, the users can have an app ready in minutes and publish it directly from the chat interface. The app gets a unique web address in the format .grok.me, where “name” usually consists of four random words. It is something of a privacy feature, to make sure people can’t just guess an app’s location easily. But according to security researchers Claroc, these addresses can be found through passive DNS services, which collect and index domain names observed in DNS traffic. In other words, anyone can find a published app even if their creator (or no one else, for that matter) ever shared a link for it. As Claroc explained in its report, the researchers did just that, identifying 43,601 addresses under grok.me. Unlocked apps But finding someone’s app shouldn’t be a big deal, right? These apps are all password-protected, right? Well, wrong. The researchers found that almost all of the apps (35,578, or 94.7%) could be accessed without authentication. That means that whatever data they were holding and generating could be accessed with almost no trouble at all. Further investigation uncovered a major oversight - when users want to publish an app, they are offered three privacy choices: “Anyone with the link”, “Invited Users”, and “Only You”. Similar to how Google Docs does it, when you want to share a document. The problem here, according to Claroc, is that “Anyone with the link” is set as the default option, suggesting that most people building apps on Grok simply weren’t paying attention to the privacy and sharing options. But still, simply accessing an app doesn’t necessarily have to be a security disaster, right? It’s just an app, right? Well, wrong again. While most apps were “harmless” in that regard (think games, calculators, landing pages), one in ten contained sensitive or internal business information, and 2% exposed information serious enough to warrant a high, or critical severity rating. Leaking information Claroc found a hospital employee directory with more than 3,500 names, an intensive care briefing containing patient information, and a trucking company’s recruitment database listing more than 1,000 individuals. It also found an employee timesheet whose downloadable code contained 18 accounts with plaintext passwords, including administrator credentials . Even SpaceXSI was leaking its own classified information this way. The researchers found 24 open apps containing onboarding plans, employee names lists, a sales territory map of almost 600 strategic accounts and their pipeline, media plans and advertiser decks (all with budget tiers, including one for a US federal agency marked as confidential), seven campaign reports for advertisers around the world, and much, much more. The researchers found one solitary app, an archive of a streaming service’s ad measurement studies, that asked for a password. Everything else was left wide open. Claroc also tested to see if they could alter the data found in these apps and built two of their own to test the theory out. One allowed unauthenticated visitor to modify a shared contact database, while another automatically granted access to anyone signing in with a Google account…
articles.author: Sead Fadilpašić

articles.title: Firefox's built-in VPN outage in Iran — Mozilla blames suspected abuse by third-party apps
articles.content: Firefox's free built-in VPN temporarily went dark for users in Iran Mozilla cited suspected third-party app abuse for the temporary disruption The service has now reportedly been restored Firefox’s free, built-in VPN went offline for some users in Iran, and Mozilla says the cause was a temporary disruption to investigate suspected abuse of the service by unauthorized third-party apps. The outage prompted complaints on social media platforms and online forums. Users in Iran said the VPN — free and one of the best VPN options in Iran because it needed no extra software — first stopped connecting and then disappeared from the browser entirely. "It appears that over the past 24 hours, Mozilla has disabled its internal VPN service for users in Iran," one X user wrote on Tuesday, a sentiment echoed across several other posts in Persian and English. VPNs are by no means a niche tool in Iran — by some estimates, roughly nine in ten Iranian internet users rely on one to bypass state filtering. So, even a brief outage of a popular, free option was quickly felt. (Image credit: Future) NEW : Leave No Trace — A weekly newsletter on digital privacy and online surveillance. Leave No Trace investigates the companies and governments putting our digital freedom at risk — and the people fighting back. 📩 Subscribe now to get every edition delivered to your inbox every Friday, launching this September. Iran's Firefox VPN outage: what we know The reports circulated first on X and Reddit, where Iranian users described losing access, before being pulled together in a Hacker News post titled "Tell HN: Firefox’s built-in VPN stopped working for some users in Iran.” According to the post, Firefox users in Iran had used the free VPN for months, even though Iran was never part of the feature’s official rollout. For many users in Iran, it offers a convenient way to reach blocked sites from a browser they already have. The free tier, introduced into Firefox in 2026 , normally comes with a monthly data allowance in exchange for signing in with a Mozilla account — and is separate from Mozilla’s paid, standalone VPN service . As it happens, Mozilla has just lifted that cap , announcing on November 10 that the built-in VPN would offer unlimited data through January 31, 2027. At first, nobody could say why the outage happened. Some users suspected the Iranian government had blocked Mozilla’s service at the network level, as it has done with other VPN providers. Others blamed Mozilla itself, suggesting it had quietly disabled access for Iranian IP addresses in order to comply with US sanctions. Comment from r/firefox The eventual answer was neither. A Mozilla spokesperson confirmed : "We recently discovered potential abuse of Firefox’s free built-in VPN by unauthorized third-party apps and temporarily disrupted access to investigate", before going on to confirm that service has since been restored. Discovering the outage was a temporary anti-abuse measure rather than a policy change targeting Iran has eventually come as a relief for affected users. What it means for people in Iran For now, the episode is a reminder of how tenuous access to the open internet can be. Using an "unauthorized" VPN has been illegal in Iran since February 2024, and users have reportedly received text messages threatening prosecution for bypassing restrictions . Iranian users do have alternatives. Proton VPN Free is a long-standing favorite, with obfuscation features built for hostile networks. Indeed, its signups from Iran have repeatedly surged during previous blackouts. There’s also Windscribe Free , which supports censorship-resistant protocols . With Iran's internet as unpredictable as ever, the last thing its users need is another trusted tool vanishing overnight.
articles.author: Mark Gill

articles.title: Developers have been hacking around MCP’s file-upload problem for two years. A fix is taking shape.
articles.content: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has played an instrumental part in connecting AI assistants to external tools and data since Anthropic launched the project some two years ago . Want to have a coding agent check the status of a bug? Give it access to your issue tracker through an MCP server. Or ask an assistant how many orders your company shipped last week? Connect it to a tool that can query your database. Part of the Agentic AI Foundation since last December , MCP has a roadmap that reflects the demands of running the protocol in production. For instance, maintainers have been working to make servers easier to deploy without keeping track of individual client sessions, and to let companies manage access through their existing identity systems. But a perennial problem developers have faced is how to pass a file from an AI app to an MCP tool. For example, say you attach a PDF to a chat and ask the assistant to save it to cloud storage — the assistant can call a tool to save the file, but developers still have to work out how to get the PDF from the chat app to the tool. That can mean issuing a temporary upload link, or perhaps sending the user to a separate upload page. To address this gap, the folks at the MCP project have outlined a draft extension that gives clients and tools a common way to handle uploads and downloads. MCP’s finally tackling the file-upload problem Why MCP needs a way to move files In a blog post published on Tuesday, Den Del i marsky , lead maintainer of MCP and member of technical staff at Anthropic, and Google software engineer Wil St. Charles , lay out the rationale for the new extension, noting that developers’ needs have changed as they’ve started asking agents to do more with the tools MCP connects them to. “Many of those MCP server projects now need to work with files — often driven by increasing agent capabilities and autonomy.” “Over the past two years, the things people build with the protocol have become more ambitious. Much more ambitious,” they write. “Many of those MCP server projects now need to work with files — often driven by increasing agent capabilities and autonomy.” This demand has shown up in the community more or less since MCP’s inception. In December 2024 , a developer building a tool to process files asked on GitHub how to get a file from the client to the server. An Anthropic team member acknowledged the difficulty and said they were exploring how a tool could send a file back to an AI app. Other community members subsequently chipped in with advice, with one noting that they had built their own way to send files from the AI app to the MCP server. Their MCP client uploaded the file directly to the server before calling the tool, with the upload itself happening outside the protocol. Developers have been looking for ways to hack around the gap ever since. In one Reddit thread a few months back, one user said a temporary S3 upload link worked in Claude once outbound access was enabled, but they couldn’t get the same approach working in ChatGPT, so they built a separate web app and upload page. Another developer said they had built a drag-and-drop interface to an MCP App, which let users submit files themselves but still left the agent without a way to initiate the upload on its own. There are packaged options, too. FastMCP offers a drag-and-drop upload component for developers building MCP Apps, while Box recently launched secure file upload and download support for PDFs and Office documents through its own MCP server. The folks at the MCP project, for their part, have been slowly working toward a common standard. Delimarsky opened an exploratory upload proposal in August 2025, and a File Uploads Working Group, initially made up of members from Anthropic and OpenAI, followed in April . articles.title: Google Lens bug traps Chrome users by hiding the close button
articles.content: TL;DR Google Lens has not been letting Chrome users close out of the side panel. The problem appears to lie with a CSS issue from a Chrome update to the Lens overlay. Google said the issue is fixed but some people still have the issue even after the latest update. Google Lens , the AI-powered search tool that lets you find what you’re looking for with images instead of words, has not been letting Chrome users close out of the feature. That should now be fixed, according to Google, though not everyone affected seems to agree. Reports on Reddit and Google’s Chrome Help Support forums started coming in about a week ago: The “x” to close out of Google Lens was missing for many. None of the usual fixes — closing tabs, shutting Chrome altogether, clearing cache and cookies, and restarting computers — worked to rectify the situation. One user who replied to a post in a Chrome sub shared a temporary solution to closing out of Lens: dragging the tab with Lens open into a new window and then dragging it back into the old window.

articles.title: Is It Worth Buying a Ceramic Apple Watch?
articles.content: The Apple Watch Series 12's ceramic casing option is its most luxurious, offering a distinctive finish and highly scratch-resistant material at a price above both aluminum and titanium. Is it worth choosing? The ceramic Apple Watch starts at $899 , compared to $399 for aluminum and $699 for titanium. Available in Pearl White and Night Blue, it brings ceramic back to the lineup for the first time since the Series 5. It is aimed at buyers who want a more unusual and special Apple Watch, and are willing to pay for the material and appearance rather than additional features. Pearl White is particularly distinctive, with a lustrous, nonmetallic finish unlike anything offered in aluminum or titanium. For earlier ceramic Apple Watch models, Apple described a manufacturing process that combined zirconia powder with alumina before molding the case, heating it to form a dense solid, and polishing it with a diamond slurry. That process produced the smooth surface and rich white appearance that helped make the ceramic Apple Watch Edition so distinctive. The included band is part of that appeal. Apple pairs the ceramic watches with exclusive Sand and Navy Blue Sport Bands featuring ceramic pin-and-tuck closures that match their respective cases. The Sand band gives the Pearl White model a distinctive overall appearance, with the matching ceramic closure providing a detail absent from ordinary Sport Bands. Ceramic also offers a different look when paired with other bands. Pearl White creates a striking contrast with darker rubber or woven bands, while Night Blue offers a more understated combination. Metal bracelets remain an option, although their connectors will contrast with the ceramic case; buyers who prefer a coordinated metallic appearance may favor titanium with a Link Bracelet or Milanese Loop. Ceramic also offers a practical benefit beyond its appearance: resistance to cosmetic wear. Earlier ceramic Apple Watch models were known for cases that were exceptionally difficult to scratch, helping preserve their finish throughout years of use. Polished titanium can pick up visible surface scratches, so buyers concerned about their watch retaining its original appearance have a good reason to consider ceramic. Ceramic can still chip or crack under forceful impact, even though it resists scratches very well. It is a luxury case material with useful durability characteristics, rather than a substitute for the Apple Watch Ultra's rugged design. Like titanium, the ceramic Series 12 features a sapphire front crystal that is highly resistant to scratches. Aluminum models instead feature Ceramic Shield 2, which refers to the front cover rather than a ceramic case. Titanium provides sapphire for $200 less, but it does not replicate the ceramic casing's distinctive finish or material qualities. The ceramic models also include cellular connectivity as standard, while aluminum models offer a choice of GPS or GPS and Cellular. The $500 difference between their starting prices therefore covers more than the case material and front crystal, although ceramic remains a substantial premium even when comparing equivalent configurations. There is a compromise in weight and proportions. Ceramic models are larger and heavier than their aluminum and titanium counterparts, without providing a larger display. The larger ceramic model weighs 51.3 grams in Pearl White and 52.9 grams in Night Blue, compared to 44.9 grams for titanium. Internally, the ceramic Apple Watch Series 12 offers the exact same chip, sensors, display technology, and battery life as the aluminum and titanium versions. It also starts at $100 more than the Apple Watch Ultra 4 , despite the Ultra offering longer battery life and additional capabilities. Aluminum remains the stronger choice for buyers focused on features and value, while titanium offers a premium metallic finish and sapphire crystal at a lower price. Ceramic is for buyers who place greater importance on…

articles.title: Scientists check their work and confirm it with update on iconic black hole image
articles.content: The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong. This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data. The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica. Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape. Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. The new approach used closed triplets (using three telescopes for error correction) rather than station pairs in an effort to reduce error. To the relief of the EHT team, the new image recreated the iconic ring-like image seen in the original, according to a paper published in Nature today . In a prepared statement, Lai said taking pictures of black holes was not easy. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the Moon," he said. He explained that when his team applied new advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to the original Event Horizon Telescope dataset, they found a black hole almost identical in size and shape to the historic EHT image. "Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data. This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process," he said. Event Horizon Telescope director Laurent Loinard welcomed the new study. "It is extremely gratifying to see that an elegant, entirely independent method recovers the ring structure of M87 across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration's published results," he said. ®
articles.author: Lindsay Clark

articles.title: What to watch tonight: 58 new shows and movies just added to Netflix, Prime Video, Hulu and more (Nov. 11)

I've gone through everything from Netflix , Prime Video , Hulu etc to see what's recently landed. I've even added some live sports you can stream on some of the best streaming services, along with movies you can watch for free on Tubi. Top picks to stream tonight ‘The Gospel of Christmas’ (2026) (Netflix) Genre: Christmas drama movie What it's about: "The Gospel of Christmas" follows Isaac (Durrell “Tank” Babbs), a struggling pastor who inherits his family’s church in a troubled New York neighborhood. Alongside his wife Rebecca (Fantasia Barrino), he attempts to rebuild the struggling congregation and protect it from a sinister adversary. But with his faith wavering and his family facing mounting challenges, Isaac must find the strength to save the church and its community before Christmas. The film boasts an impressive lineup of gospel talent, including Fantasia Barrino, Tank, CeCe Winans, Yolanda Adams and The Clark Sisters. With Kirk Franklin producing the soundtrack, there's plenty to look forward to on the musical front, with some powerful vocal performances adding to its uplifting story. Five years after the fall of Eregion, the Dark Lord is secretly working to forge the One Ring, which he hopes will give him control over all life. Meanwhile, Elves, Dwarves, Men and Wizards must unite to stop his growing power before he achieves total domination. Why you should watch it: "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" continues to deliver the kind of sweeping fantasy adventure that's perfect for a weekend binge. Season 3 raises the stakes with impressive battle sequences, stunning visuals and a darker story as Sauron continues his rise to power. If you've been waiting for another reason to return to Middle-earth, this latest season is a strong excuse. Watch "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" S3 on Prime Video now ‘Rivals’ (season 2 part 2 premiere) (Hulu) Genre: Period comedy-drama series What it's about: In part two of "Rivals" season 2, the battle between rival television companies Corinium and Venturer reaches boiling point following Lady Monica Baddingham’s tragic death. Tony (David Tennant) becomes increasingly ruthless, while Rupert (Alex Hassell) faces difficult decisions about his future with Taggie (Bella Maclean). As affairs unravel, family secrets emerge and new alliances form, the residents of Rutshire find themselves caught up in even more scandal. Why you should watch it: "Rivals" returns for season 2 with even more scandal and messy relationship drama. There's no shortage of outrageous affairs, bitter rivalries and unexpected twists in these new episodes, all set against the show's wonderfully flashy 1980s backdrop. It's gloriously over-the-top entertainment and an easy binge if you enjoy your period dramas with a healthy dose of chaos. articles.title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
articles.content: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey. COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20. This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31. In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked. This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations. Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.” So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage. Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.) The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country). Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal. Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support. One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there. The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a…

articles.title: Validating GPU Platforms with Runtime AI Inventory via the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory
articles.content: As teams deploy and scale AI workloads using NVIDIA Dynamo, Kubeflow, or Slurm, tracking what actually runs requires visibility beyond the platform... As teams deploy and scale AI workloads using NVIDIA Dynamo, Kubeflow, or Slurm, tracking what actually runs requires visibility beyond the platform configuration captured in a recipe. Application teams define and update these workloads independently of the platform recipe, so a reproducible deployment bundle alone cannot establish which workload artifacts are running on each node. Source

articles.title: Google Gemini now lets you see everything it remembers about you — here's how to take control
articles.content: Google has spent the past year making Gemini smarter, more capable and better connected to the apps and services people use every day. But one of its most useful features might also be one of its most personal: memory. As Gemini has evolved, it's gotten better at remembering details from previous conversations, picking up where you left off and helping with ongoing projects. That's convenient, especially if you use the chatbot regularly, but it also raises an important question: How much does Gemini actually remember about you? Until now, managing Gemini's memory hasn't always been straightforward. Google has offered controls for reviewing and deleting chat activity, but understanding what the chatbot has learned about you is another matter. That's where Gemini's new Memory summary comes in. The feature gives users a clearer look at the information Gemini remembers about them, along with the ability to make changes. Here's how to find your Memory summary, see what Gemini remembers and take control of the information it uses to personalize your conversations. Now you can see what Gemini remembers about you and actually edit it (Image credit: Shutterstock) Google has begun rolling out its new “Memory summary” feature in Gemini for users who work with the chatbot through its desktop and mobile browser versions (it doesn’t seem to be working with the mobile Gemini app at the moment, however). And with this update comes the ability for users to take a look at what Gemini remembers about them and edit it to add more details about themselves or delete it as a whole. The Memory summary doesn’t just feature a massive info dump that’s all about you—it actually summarizes everything it remembers about you via bullet points that detail your background, relationships, work, interests and preferences. After observing everything Gemini has learned about you and retained as the data it has gained from your previous conversations. (Image credit: Future) I actually used my personal Gemini account to see how this new feature works. Accessing it on desktop and through your mobile browser is as simple as going to your “Settings” and clicking on “Personal Intelligence” to be led to the “Memory” and “Memory summary” tabs. You can toggle the Memory tab to let Gemini keep retaining information about you or stop it from performing that action. I clicked on the Memory summary tab and this is the summarized information it has collected about me so far (I’ll be sure to add more information about my profession at some point): (Image credit: Future) Google has stated that the Memory feature is only available to Gemini users in the US who are over the age of 18 and have an active Google AI plan. Also, those users must have the “Keep activity” and “Memory” options enabled. But in my case, I got to play around with the Memory feature through my free Gemini subscription plan. Bottom line AI users have already gotten hip to the fact that most chatbots can bring up past details from their past conversations and use that information to generate more personalized answers to their questions & prompts. It’s nice to see Google allow Gemini users to not only get a full picture of what its chatbot has learned and remembered about them, but also give those same users the opportunity to add, change or delete those details. articles.title: Fitbit users’ metrics are missing from Google Health — and there’s no fix
articles.content: Fitbit users’ daily metrics are missing from the Google Health app The issue might have been caused by a software update Google says a fix is not coming ‘in the immediate future’ Users of the best Fitbit devices are reporting that several key health metrics have gone missing from the Google Health app synced to their wearables , with stats like heart-rate variability, blood oxygen and more nowhere to be found. And it gets worse, as Google has admitted that there might not be a fix for some time to come. The issue came to light on social media , where multiple threads have sprung up full of users frustrated that, instead of their usual complement of stats, many metrics are simply reading 'No data.' Based on the reports, the problem seems to be affecting breathing rate, blood-oxygen levels, resting heart rate, skin-temperature variation, and more. For some people, their Fitbit device was still able to record their sleep stats overnight, and previous days’ metrics continue to show up. However, more recent data compiled in the Vitals section is what appears to be affected. This will no doubt be a frustrating occurrence for Fitbit users wanting to keep up with their latest health metrics. Yet further investigation appears to have revealed a potential culprit. Google responds (Image credit: Fitbit) Back on Reddit, Fitbit’s 5.12 update has been suggested as the potential cause of the problem. “After the 5.12 update this particular issue started to arise,” one person noted , before asking: “did you update the app recently?” For some, uninstalling the Google Health app and then reinstalling it fixed the problem. Unfortunately, one Redditor pointed out that you might have to do that every morning, as the metrics in the Vitals section reset with each day. Alternatively, signing out of the app and signing back in might be enough to put things right. Another suggestion was to switch each metric’s chart from weekly to monthly and then back to weekly. Google hasn’t remained entirely silent throughout this situation. A member of the company’s support staff informed one Redditor that Google is aware of the problem and that “We’ll continue to monitor the situation, and keep our team informed of the impact to you and other customers.” What Google didn’t do, however, was promise a remedy. As the company support rep said of the metrics bug, “We’re aware of it, but may not be able to provide a fix in the immediate future … We understand that this isn’t the resolution you’re hoping for, but rest assured we’re always working to improve our products.” One frustrated commenter summed up Google’s response this way: “Ridiculous that a multi-trillion-dollar company can’t fix an issue when they have AI that are coded to actually fix things like this and top-of-the-line engineering.” With no fix on the way any time soon and a wide variety of potential cures mooted on social media, it’s difficult for anyone affected by this issue to know what to do to get their metrics back. For now, perhaps the best you can do is try the solutions mentioned earlier and keep your fingers crossed that Google takes action sooner rather than later.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s involvement with an alleged Chinese spy is the stuff of Hollywood thrillers. These 10, for example
articles.content: The billionaire CEO of one of the world’s most successful companies is drawn into an affair with an alluring, jet-setting businesswoman. He becomes closer and shares more—only to discover that she’s secretly a Chinese spy. It sounds like the plot of a Hollywood blockbuster. But a version of that plotline is allegedly unfolding for real inside NVIDIA , the world’s second most valuable company. CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who is accused of working with the Chinese government . NVIDIA’s board says it’s still investigating the allegations, and that it has no reason to believe trade secrets were compromised. Hollywood, meanwhile, has been exploring the “honey trap” plot for nearly a century. Here are ten notable examples. 1. The Americans (2013-2018) FX’s critically acclaimed spy drama offers a multi-layered portrayal of the long-term honey trap. Keri Russell and Matthew Rhys star as Elizabeth and Philip Jennings, Soviet spies infiltrating America during the Cold War. Most honey trap plots portray a female spy as the seducer. The Americans flips the script–with devastating results. 2. Red Sparrow (2018) Jennifer Lawrence plays Dominika Egorova, a Russian ballerina recruited into a secret intelligence program. Pursuing a CIA operative and carefully controlled by her Russian handlers, Egorova discovers that the manipulation of a honey trap agent can go both ways. 3. Lust, Caution (2007) The honey trap is a staple of Western spy films. But the same basic plotline cuts across cultures. In this film from Ang Lee, Tang Wei portrays a young woman who is recruited by a resistance organization during the Japanese occupation of China.Her mission is to arrange for her target’s assassination, but feelings begin to get in the way. 4. Notorious (1946) Alfred Hitchcock’s 1946 film is proof that the honey trap has fascinated screenwriters and directors for generations. With a legendary cast, including Ingrid Bergman and Cary Grant, Notorious explores what happens when a honey trap becomes a love triangle. 5. The Little Drummer Girl (2018) Although Hollywood has provided especially fertile ground to depict honey traps on the screen, the idea of a honey trap is a staple of the spy novel, too. Case in point: John le Carre’s espionage thriller, which was adapted for the screen as The Little Drummer Girl . The miniseries depicts a young recruit of the Israeli intelligence forces tasked with infiltrating a Palestinian militant organization, blurring the lines between fake and real identities. 6. Black Book (2006) This Paul Verhoeven film is set in the Nazi occupied Netherlands during World War 2. Tasked with infiltrating German intelligence circles, Jewish operative Rachel Stein (Carice van Houten) begins to question the real loyalties of those around her. 7. The Handmaiden (2016) Most honey traps involve spies and the clandestine world of espionage. But some explore the same general idea in less secretive places. South Korean filmmaker Park Chan-Wook’s 2016 film depicts a young pickpocket who is recruited to help a con artist seduce a wealthy heiress. It quickly becomes unclear, though, who is manipulating whom. 8. M. Butterfly (1993) Much of what happens in the top secret world of espionage remains exactly that: top secret. But occasionally real-life spy dramas are declassified. When that happens, they often make great material for a Hollywood story. That’s the case with this film about a diplomat who is seduced by a Chinese opera singer. Inspired by real events, the film shows how even a high-level figure can be drawn into a honey trap. 9. From Russia With Love (1963) James Bond may be able to skydive into a falling airplane or windsurf a tsunami , but even he can fall prey to the honey trap. The classic Bond film From Russia With Love centers around Soviet clerk Tatiana Romanova, who appears willing to defect–and draws bond into a romantic…

articles.title: Google Home bug leaves Nest camera notifications without video previews
articles.content: TL;DR Nest camera users report missing video previews and thumbnails in Android notifications. The issue affects multiple phones and Nest camera models, though previews still work on some other devices. Cameras continue recording normally; it’s just the previews that are missing. We’ve reached out to Google for clarification. Nest camera users are reporting a frustrating bug that’s causing video previews and thumbnails on Android to disappear from notifications. This is leaving users who have gotten in the habit of quickly glancing over their camera feeds through previews with no choice but to open the Google Home app. For those unaware, Google Home’s camera notifications include a thumbnail or a short video preview to highlight what triggered the alert. This makes it easier to determine whether the alert was triggered by something routine or something that needs more attention via the Google Home app. With previews now missing , users are being forced to default to the latter option.

articles.title: Canonical web services get stage fright ahead of Ubuntu Summit
articles.content: A swathe of Canonical's web services has been offline for hours, an awkward warm-up for tomorrow's Ubuntu Summit. Canonical's status page lists widespread disruption beginning at approximately 1100 UTC, affecting gopkg.in, Ubuntu cloud images and mailing lists, jaas.ai, the Ubuntu keyserver, Launchpad PPAs, the Livepatch API, canonical.com, Ubuntu login, maas.io, and 16 other services. Landscape is also affected. Email and the company's Discourse forums remain available. The Register has asked Canonical for more information but had received no response at publication time. The company suffered a DDoS attack last month , although the cause of this outage has not been confirmed. The timing is unfortunate. As the banner across the top of the Discourse forum page says: "The Ubuntu Summit starts tomorrow – join from anywhere!" The online event runs on November 12-13. For the first time since the 2022 Summit in Prague, The Reg FOSS desk won't be attending in person. Canonical is still experimenting with the format of the event, and the last few have been primarily online, with just a small in-person audience in its London offices. This is the second of two Summits this year, labeled 26.04 and 26.10 to mirror Ubuntu's release cycle. The timetable , hosted on the Discourse site, lists several talks on AI and agentic coding. The AI-heavy program we reported from June's event appears to be continuing. ®
articles.author: Liam Proven

articles.title: OpenAI is sunsetting ChatGPT Advanced and Standard voice next month
articles.content: Credit: Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority TL;DR OpenAI has announced that it will retire ChatGPT Advanced and Standard voice on December 11, 2026. The company is focusing on unifying the voice experience through GPT-Live. Live video and screen sharing will continue to use Advanced voice until GPT-Live has this capability. Earlier this year, OpenAI rolled out a new voice model called GPT-Live . The Gemini Live rival joined ChatGPT Advanced and Standard voice as yet another way to have more natural conversations with the chatbot. As the saying goes, three is a crowd, and OpenAI is ready to do some streamlining. OpenAI has announced that a big change is coming for ChatGPT Voice. On December 11, 2026, the company will be retiring Advanced and Standard voice. The focus will now be on unifying the voice experience through GPT-Live.

articles.title: OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit over $30 billion AI data center
articles.content: Residents of Effingham County, Georgia, just filed a RICO lawsuit against their county commissioners, county leaders, and OpenAI and its affiliates, alleging that they committed various offenses in a conspiracy to get OpenAI’s “Project Camellia” approved. According to the Effingham Herald , the plaintiffs — Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr., and Raymond Carver — are seeking civil damages, saying that the project has harmed their property values and even pointing out that purchase offers for nearby residential properties have dropped or been withdrawn since the data center was announced. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible The lawsuit names all Effingham County Commissioners — Chairperson Damon Rahn, Forrest Floyd, Roger Burdette, Jamie DeLoach, Elizabeth Helmly, and Phil Kieffer — as defendants, alongside County Manager Tim Callanan, Effingham County Industrial Development Authority (IDA) CEO Brandt Herndon, the IDA itself, OpenAI, Octans GA LLC, the entity operating the data center on behalf of OpenAI, and Savannah Industrial Development LLC, the agency involved in the sale of IDA property to Octans and OpenAI. It’s alleged that the defendants committed fraud and concealment through non-disclosure agreements and misleading public statements so that residents remain unaware of the nature of the projects for as long as possible, and that there was a civil conspiracy “to advance Project Camellia through confidential negotiations and closed-door decisions.” They also claimed that the parties engaged in improper land transactions, zoning violations, and civil racketeering.w Project Camellia is one of OpenAI’s biggest data center projects planned for construction in Effingham County. The site is expected to cost somewhere between $20 billion and $30 billion, to be built across five phases, with a planned compute capacity of 3.2 gigawatts. The company also promised that it will not affect the community’s utility costs, as it will pay for the full cost of all its required infrastructure upgrades, and that it will have minimal water use due to its closed-loop water system. Despite those promises, it seems that some people are opposing the project because of how the county had allegedly tried to secure the land, tax incentives, and zoning approvals without informing the residents until key decisions were finalized and contracts had been signed. The RICO Act — or Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act — was originally conceived as a way to counter organized crime, particularly Mafia leadership, who often used low-level members to commit individual crimes and do the dirty work for them. However, Georgia’s RICO Act is less stringent than the federal version, which is why it’s been used multiple times for cases that seemingly had nothing to do with the Mafia. For example, it was in the 2023 election racketeering case against Donald Trump and 18 others in the attempt to overturn the 2020 U.S. presidential election results in the state, and it was also used in Young Thug’s trial after the rapper was accused of running YSL Records as a criminal street gang. Critics say that Georgia’s version is way too encompassing, though, and that it was being used to squeeze defendants involved in more mundane or common felonies. “When you have a hammer, everything looks like a nail,” Georgia State University professor of criminal justice and criminology Volkan Topalli said in Atlanta Magazine . The actions of both state officials, OpenAI, and its affiliates are not new, though. There have already been multiple complaints of data center developers…

articles.title: This new blood test claims to detect over 50 cancers before onset of symptoms
articles.content: Cancer isn’t the leading cause of death in the United States ; heart disease ranks first in that regard. But it’s cancer that strikes fear into the hearts of many Americans. Cancer can take an excruciating toll on its millions of victims and their family members. Cancer treatments are often highly toxic, and the disease is increasingly striking people at younger ages , which is why it accounts for more years of potential life lost than heart disease. So when a blood test comes along that claims to be able to screen for over 50 cancers at once in a single blood draw before symptoms appear—as is the case for the Galleri test , by the biotech company GRAIL—it might seem like society has a Holy Grail of modern medicine at their fingertips. But a closer look at the evidence suggests that the Galleri test is not yet the universal screening breakthrough patients and doctors hope for. As a physician who studies early cancer detection , and as chair of the American Cancer Society’s screening guideline development group , I have been following this test’s development with interest. While the Galleri test certainly shows great promise, clinical trial data indicates that it struggles with early-stage cancer detection and has not yet been shown to lower the risk of death from cancer or prevent advanced cancer. Across all cancer stages, the test missed over two-thirds of cancer cases. On Sept. 23, 2026, an advisory panel to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration voted to recommend approval of the Galleri test. While a recommendation from the FDA’s advisory panel is not the same as full approval from the agency, it marks a critical first step in the process of potentially making the test widely available to the American public. The FDA has not yet announced when it will make a decision on the test. But even as the advisory panel approved the test, panelists recommended that the word “early” be removed from “early cancer detection test” in product labeling. Panel members were not convinced the test can find cancers at their earliest and most curable stages, and they expressed uncertainty about the test’s benefit to patients at this time. Given this uncertainty, careful scrutiny of the data behind the test can help doctors and patients make informed decisions about whether to use it. What is the Galleri test? How does it work? Galleri is part of an emerging class of multicancer early detection tests . These tests do not diagnose cancer: If a test is positive, further evaluation is necessary to determine whether cancer is present, and, if so, what type of cancer. It is offered as a screening test, similar to mammography for breast cancer screening or PSA testing for prostate cancer screening, but with the potential advantage of screening for many cancers at once, including many for which no screening test currently exists. The Galleri test looks for DNA fragments in blood that are associated with cancer. When something goes wrong with your DNA, whether because you inherited a mutation or something in your environment triggered that mutation, the processes that regulate cell division can go awry. Uncontrolled cell division can trigger the growth of cancer cells. Galleri and other multicancer early detection tests in development look for differences that distinguish the DNA produced by tumor cells from normal cells. Galleri identifies unique tags on cancer DNA called methylation markers and uses machine learning algorithms to generate a positive or negative test result. What are the strengths of the Galleri test? The Galleri test looks for DNA signals from over 50 cancers , including the 12 that account for almost two-thirds of cancer deaths in the U.S , such as lung and pancreas cancer. Importantly, it provides information on which organ the possible tumor likely originated from. Currently recommended cancer screenings are largely limited to four types of cancer. Many of the cancers the Galleri test looks for are not currently included in…

articles.title: Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick
articles.content: This blog post focuses on how AI can improve and expedite the product development life cycle using agents built on AWS Quick, with human approval baked into the process. AI-driven software delivery is helping teams ship products faster than ever. As implementation accelerates, the upstream product development process becomes even more important. Coding agents can turn clear requirements into working software faster than before, but they can’t compensate for building the wrong product. With implementation becoming easier, your competitive advantage moves upstream to four critical activities: discovering the right customer problem, deciding which opportunity to pursue, designing the right experience, and validating it through a prototype. The signals that you need to make those decisions are scattered everywhere. Your customers leave feedback in Slack, your sales team logs insights in Salesforce, systems record incidents in ServiceNow, stakeholders document requirements in Microsoft SharePoint, engineers track work items in Jira, and teams make decisions in Outlook meetings and email threads. As your teams move between these tools, they disconnect context from the decisions it should inform, and lose more at every handoff. AWS Quick provides the connective layer for this fragmented knowledge. By grounding custom chat agents in connected enterprise data and storing their artifacts in shared Spaces , AWS Quick helps your team build with existing organizational knowledge instead of starting each initiative from a blank page. The AI-Driven Product Development Lifecycle (AI-PDLC) is a framework that applies these capabilities through a suite of six AWS Quick agents with specialized skills, producing a traceable set of artifacts at each phase. Agents gather and structure context, surface gaps, and draft artifacts. You and your team contribute judgment and approve every decision. The objective isn’t to produce documents faster. It’s to help your team think better, preserve why each decision was made, and give engineering and coding agents a specification grounded in customer evidence. We will show you how to configure the six-agent AI-PDLC suite in AWS Quick and use it to move from distributed customer signals to a validated prototype. Throughout, it preserves context from the first insight through the engineering handoff. Architecture The diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the AI-PDLC framework. Figure 1: End-to-end AI-PDLC flow, from scattered enterprise signals through AWS Quick agents to the coding-agent handoff It starts with the signals most teams lose track of, that is, the Slack threads, Jira tickets, docs, and call transcripts that hold the why behind a decision and what customers actually said. Enterprise connectors pull that context from Slack, Outlook, Jira, Salesforce, SharePoint, ServiceNow, and many more enterprise sources. Figure 2: AWS Quick builds a personal knowledge graph that links people, projects, and decisions across connected apps and folders AWS Quick can build a personal knowledge graph from your connected apps and folders, linking the people, projects, and decisions across your tools. Those signals feed the brain: the set of agents on AWS Quick, led by an Orchestrator that runs Discovery, Prioritize, Working Backwards, Spec Generator, and Designer. Everything they produce lands in one common language: a prototype_spec.md holding the acceptance criteria, personas, screens, data model. Every decision traces back to a source. AWS Quick can delegate development tasks to AI coding agents using the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) . ACP is an open JSON-RPC 2.0 standard with no vendor lock-in. Customers can use their preferred coding agent like Kiro or Claude Code to build against the specification generated by AI-PDLC. Underneath it all runs a human approval gate at every stage. You validate the pain points, approve priorities, sign off the spec, gate the build, and accept the review. Production data then flows back…

articles.title: The Next Pandemic May Not Infect Humans
articles.content: We keep connecting software and giving AI agents more room to act. I think that changes how attacks can spread. October has been a rough month for anyone trying to keep software secure. PHP disclosed critical vulnerabilities . Node.js released security fixes, with the most serious rated High . Zeabur reported an intrusion involving leaked internal credentials , and LiteLLM's official release pipeline published a compromised package and container images . By the end of the month, Polymarket had reported a third-party compromise affecting its international platform , and Binance had disclosed a theft of about $6.3 billion . These are separate incidents. Some are vulnerability disclosures, and some are actual breaches. I haven't seen evidence that they were coordinated, or that AI agents caused all of them. Looking at them together, though, I keep noticing how much of our security depends on other people's systems staying trustworthy. A package comes through the official release channel. A cloud platform holds credentials for infrastructure we run. A third-party script runs on a page where people manage money. Most days those connections work, so we stop thinking about them. Now, we're adding AI agents that read across those systems and act on what they find. I'm less worried about whether an agent can be tricked once. I'm more worried about whether it can pass the trick on. We've Seen This Before In 2017, WannaCry spread through vulnerable computers and disrupted hospitals, businesses, and public services. NotPetya started with a compromised software update and spread through corporate networks, causing damage far beyond its first targets. Neither attack had to reach every victim on its own. They moved through connections that already existed. Modern software has a lot of those. Even a small application can rely on hundreds of packages, an outside login provider, several APIs, cloud infrastructure, and an automated deployment pipeline. A developer may depend on a package they have never read because some other package needs it. That isn't necessarily careless. No team can build and audit everything it uses, and shared software is a big reason small teams can ship anything at all. The cost is that when a trusted component fails, the damage can reach systems whose owners never chose to trust the original source. AI didn't create this problem. It does change how much software we produce, how fast we connect it, and how much those connections are allowed to do. More Software to Secure Someone with little programming experience can now describe an application to a coding agent and have something working in an afternoon. I get why people are excited. An idea that used to stay in a notebook can turn into a working tool before dinner. Trouble starts when "it works" gets treated as "I understand what was built." An agent can pick dependencies, write authentication logic, configure database access, and set deployment permissions along with the parts you can see. Those choices still need review, even if the person accepting them didn't realize they were choices. A missing authorization check won't show up on any screen. A credential can have far more access than the app needs. An unnecessary dependency won't make a single test fail. Experienced engineers miss these things too, and handwritten code isn't automatically safer. What's different now is volume. We can produce a lot more code, and the attention available to review it hasn't grown at the same rate. Put simply, writing software is getting cheaper faster than understanding, securing, and maintaining it. For a prototype that never leaves a laptop, that may be fine. For an app holding customer data, or a tool wired into a company's internal systems, somebody inherits the gap, usually whoever has to run it later. Attackers get the same discount. AI can help them generate variations of malicious code, adapt scripts to different environments, and automate parts of their research. Most…

articles.title: Why Nitric stopped asking one AI agent to do everything
articles.content: We’re a team of five engineers, and we used to wake the on-call engineer three or four times a week over production incidents. Most were noise rather than serious outages, but at two in the morning, being overly cautious seemed preferable to letting a genuine problem slip through the cracks. We’ve since reduced both unnecessary overnight interruptions and recurring issues by iterating on triage and following investigations through to fixes. Specialized AI agents help us investigate incidents, organize follow-up work, and prepare changes, with engineers reviewing and correcting the work along the way. What surprised us was how much more comfortable we became relying on the process. Engineers could inspect an assessment, challenge its assumptions, and use those corrections to improve how we handled later incidents. As follow-up fixes addressed recurring issues, we felt more confident about when to wake the on-call engineer. That experience has made us question the shape of the work we give our agents. A capable coding agent could potentially investigate an incident, raise a ticket, and prepare a fix, so why divide those responsibilities? “When an agent’s work needs correction, can you identify the responsibility involved and make a change you can evaluate independently?” For us, it’s about improving one part of the workflow and judging whether the change helped. When an agent’s work needs correction, can you identify the responsibility involved and make a change you can evaluate independently? A shared workspace for people and agents We’re building Sugabots as an open-source, self-hosted workspace where a team can work with several agents on the same task. Engineers can ask questions, contribute evidence, review findings, and bring in another agent, with those exchanges available to other participants. We organize that work into shared environments called pods, with connections to external systems through MCP . Each agent can have its own model and instructions, while the pod’s connections and tool policies define the access its agents share. The team can configure agents for specific responsibilities and refine their instructions as engineers review the work. Our incident workflow has helped us explore which responsibilities benefit from that separation. How we run incident triage in Sugabots Our incident workflow depends on each engineer or agent being able to continue from the evidence, decisions, and corrections recorded during the investigation. Our Sentry triage agent investigates new, regressed, or escalating issues and decides whether to alert the on-call engineer , request an in-hours review, hand a small fix directly to an implementation agent, or keep the issue in Sentry for monitoring. It records follow-up work in Linear, where a backlog agent helps organize tickets, and the implementation agent can prepare a GitHub pull request for review. Our incident workflow: agents handle distinct responsibilities while engineers contribute to the shared investigation. Engineers can take on any of the contributions shown. Engineers participate throughout, reviewing findings, challenging urgency assessments, correcting assumptions, and deciding whether to ship a proposed change. The investigation remains available as work moves between people and agents. Safeguards back that growing confidence. The instructions call for urgent escalation when an issue could plausibly be a production outage, and urgency is uncertain. Issues classified as noise are archived until escalating, and Sentry retains a direct spike-alert route to incident.io as a backup. The follow-up matters as much as the initial assessment. Previously, the on-call engineer might investigate an alert, determine it could wait until office hours, and return to other work. Recording the underlying problem in the backlog and prioritizing it gave the team a chance to resolve it before the next on-call engineer…

articles.title: Amazon's Ring Unveils Flying Drone and Robot To Patrol Homes and Businesses
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from CNBC: Amazon's Ring is going deeper into surveillance with an indoor drone for home monitoring and an autonomous robot designed to patrol businesses. The company on Tuesday unveiled the $250 Ring Drone Cam, a security camera that can fly from room to room, including upstairs, as well as capture footage during the day or at night. When an alarm or sensor on windows, doors and home security devices is triggered, the textbook-sized drone travels a preset path to investigate suspicious activity. Users can also deploy the drone at any time, the company said. [...] The company on Tuesday also debuted the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam. The device repurposes Amazon's Astro home robot, which had a short life as a business device and has seen few upgrades since its 2021 debut, for companies to use to patrol offices, warehouses and other workspaces. Ring said it "leveraged the best of Astro" to build the Ring Rover Cam, which it describes as a "purpose-built security robot." Similar to the Astro, the device is a display mounted on a two-wheeled base with an extendable periscope camera. It also features a "built-in siren," two-way audio and a "light tower" that shines onto the ceiling to help users keep track of its whereabouts. The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: PC peripheral maker Logitech giving all of its 7,000 employees the day off to play GTA 6
articles.content: As GTA 6, the most anticipated game of the year, perhaps the decade, nears its November 19 release date , one company has offered its employees the chance to take the day off to play it. Amid the expectation that gamers around the globe will call in sick to play the game instead of heading into the office, PC peripheral and hardware outfit Logitech is getting ahead of the game by giving 7,000 employees the chance to take a day off to play it. Or, if they prefer, they can play any other game instead, the company confirmed in a press release detailing the move. The new initiative is called "Logi Game Day," and it isn't only available to the top brass. Interns and full-time employees alike can take a day off from now until this time next year, at a time when it's been estimated that the GTA 6 launch could see the U.S. economy take a $1 billion hit in terms of productivity. The game, which is a console exclusive ahead of a claimed early 2027 PC release , is already available for preorder, with pre-loading also up and running. It's a good job, too, with a 212GB PS5 download set to be a real downer for eager gamers with slow internet. The ongoing price hikes also mean that upgrading your PS5 storage for GTA 6 won't be a fun time, either. As for Logitech, the company believes that it's time for people to move away from the belief that playing games is a waste of time, hence its new initiative. It makes sense for a company that makes gaming accessories to say that, of course, but CEO Hanneke Faber argues that the company sees "how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other.” The hope will be that, by allowing employees to play games, a productivity boost will follow. Whether that comes to fruition remains to be seen. But there's less doubt about GTA 6's popularity a little more than a week out from its release. If you've yet to get your order in, you can also grab Grand Theft Auto VI for $79.99 now. You'll get a box with a code that you'll need to redeem on your PS5 to be able to download and play the game. The game's release brings an end to years of rumors and leaks, not to mention legal battles. Take-Two hit Microsoft with a subpoena in relation to a massive leak earlier this year in an attempt to find the perpetrator. Rockstar Games addressed the leaks in a post on the X social network shortly after the subpoena was made public, saying that it "would be an understatement to say that having videos of Grand Theft Auto VI gameplay leak in this way has been heartbreaking for our team."

articles.title: Marktechpost AI Launches GPU Leaderboard and the Deploy It Chrome Extension
articles.content: Marktechpost has launched GPU Leaderboard , a free cloud GPU price comparison for AI inference. It also shipped GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It , a Chrome extension for the same data. The site reads on-demand and spot prices from each provider’s own pricing page. The goal is simple: answer “what GPU do I need, and where is it cheapest?” in one place. What is GPU Leaderboard? GPU Leaderboard is a pricing dashboard that ranks rentable cloud GPUs by price per GPU-hour. It is built for teams running inference. The v1 application has 4 views: Inference pricing: a cost calculator for a full run, not a single hourly rate. Leaderboard : every offer ranked by $/GPU-hr, filterable by GPU, tier, region and availability. Cheapest Inference : the lowest on-demand floor for each tracked GPU. Providers : a directory with instance counts, regions, status-page incidents and price-check history. How does the GPU inference cost calculator work? You pick an accelerator, GPU count, duration and utilization. The calculator then prices that exact run at every provider. An optional model field narrows the list. The default example is 8×H100 for 72 hours at 90% utilization. That bills 576 GPU-hours. The cheapest result is $967.68 at Latitude, at $1.68 per GPU-hour. The median across 15 providers is $1,716.48. The most expensive is $3,545.28 at CoreWeave. The calculator also shows a “real” cost per used GPU-hour. Idle time is still billed, so $1.68 at 90% utilization becomes $1.87. This is the number most budget sheets miss. What does the Deploy It Chrome extension do? GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It brings the price data to where developers pick models. Per its store listing, it works in 3 places: Hugging Face model pages: detects model size and estimates VRAM at FP16, INT8 and INT4. It then shows the cheapest hourly GPUs that fit. GitHub repos: detects model references and gives a hardware estimate in place. Toolbar lookup: search any model or GPU from the browser toolbar. Key Takeaways GPU Leaderboard ranks 201 live GPU offers from 24 providers by $/GPU-hr. Its calculator prices a full run, including idle time at your utilization. Deploy It shows VRAM needs and cheapest GPUs on Hugging Face and GitHub. An 8×H100, 72-hour run spans $967.68 to $3,545.28 across multiple providers. Coverage and daily refresh are the main gaps versus older trackers. Try it at gpuleaderboard.com and install the Deploy It extension from the Chrome Web Store. articles.title: UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents
articles.content: Teams building AI agents on AWS use a range of frameworks, including LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each framework records agent execution in its own way, so the structure of messages, tool calls, and handoffs between agents differs from one to the next. Evaluation tooling tends to follow the same boundaries: teams build metrics, scoring logic, and result storage against a single framework’s trace format, and they must rebuild them when they switch frameworks or run agents on more than one. This coupling makes a basic development question harder to answer: did a change to the prompt, model, or tools improve the agent? Answering it requires consistent metrics across versions of an agent and a shared record of past results to compare against. Agent quality also spans several dimensions that a single accuracy score does not capture: tool calling, response quality, responsible AI, performance, multi-turn conversation, multi-agent coordination, and reasoning. In this post, we introduce the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF). Customers across 12 organizations in the telecom, healthcare, and financial services industries used UAEF to evaluate their AI agents with one consistent set of metrics and compare agent versions before release. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system: it uses adapters to convert traces from each framework into a common format, then scores those traces with 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions. It stores the results in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and generates reports and insights that inform the next iteration of the agent. This post describes how UAEF works, provides a playbook for choosing metrics and preparing datasets, and points to runnable notebooks for each supported framework. UAEF: One evaluation layer for agent frameworks UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system for AI agents. It takes the agent a team already has and scores it the same way across supported frameworks and runtimes. UAEF takes two inputs: the agent under test and a dataset to run it on. The dataset provides the inputs for each test case, and it can also include ground-truth answers, the expected output for each input. Ground truth is optional, and only metrics that compare the agent’s response against a reference use it. To evaluate tool calling, the ground truth must also include the expected tool calls for each test case: which tools the agent should call, in what order, and with what arguments. Everything after that happens inside the UAEF. Figure 1 shows the path a single evaluation takes, from the inputs to the reports and insights. First, an adapter reads the agent’s native execution, its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs, and normalizes it into one canonical trace, so that the steps that follow are identical no matter which framework produced the agent. Next, UAEF screens the trace for personally identifiable information (PII), such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers, before data is stored. The evaluation engine then scores the trace on a selection from 36 built-in metrics across 7 quality dimensions. When you persist a run, UAEF records it as an experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3: Amazon DynamoDB holds the per-experiment metadata used for listing and comparison, and Amazon S3 holds the full results. With runs stored, a team can compare an agent version against a baseline to detect regressions and generate reports and insights that explain what changed and why. Those reports close the loop: the team evaluates the agent, learns what regressed or improved, changes the prompt, model, or tools, and evaluates again. Figure 1: UAEF closed-loop evaluation data flow The rest of this section follows that flow in order: the adapters that make UAEF framework-agnostic, the evaluation engine and its metrics, PII detection, experiment storage and comparison, and the reports that close the loop.…
