articles.title: Chinese researchers set new data records for 'hollow-core' fiber tech
articles.content: Chinese researchers report major hollow-core fiber upgrades Transmission capacities of 64Tbps were reached The technology could replace solid-core fiber in infrastructure networks No matter how fast your broadband (or 5G) connection is, it could always be faster , and 'hollow-core' fiber could help. Researchers in China have now set new records for the technology, demonstrating two-way, high-speed data transmission across a distance of 1,007 kilometers (626 miles). As reported by CCTV (via Interesting Engineering ), a transmission capacity of 64 terabits per second (Tbps) was achieved in each direction, enough to download 160 films in 4K resolution (50GB each) every second — so perfect for movie night. Individual signals took just 3.43 milliseconds to travel the whole length of the link. The transmission distance is some 50 times greater than previous hollow-core trials of the same type, while latency was reduced by 30%, too. Signal-to-noise ratios and loss margins were also improved , according to the team from the China Telecom Research Institute, Yangtze Optical Fibre and Cable (YOFC), and ZTE Corporation. It's a technology that companies are already investing in. For example, last year Microsoft signed a deal with Corning and Heraeus to scale up production of hollow-core fiber in order to upgrade its Azure cloud platform. By the end of this year, around 15,000 kilometers (9,321 miles) of hollow-core fiber should be in place supporting Azure. A core change Microsoft is one of the companies already investing in hollow-core fiber (Image credit: The Silicon Review) As you can guess from the name, hollow-core fiber replaces the glass of solid-core fiber with air that has a glass lattice surrounding it. The glass edges keep optical signals heading in the right direction, but the hollow core means there's less resistance to the light — which results in faster transmission speeds and lower latency. The technology is better suited to large infrastructure projects than the cabling that connects your broadband network to your home, but you'll still feel the benefit in the coming years: data centers are already making use of the technology, and it's been tipped to support cellular networks too in the future. Several challenges remain, because hollow-core fiber is more challenging to make and install than solid-core fiber, the current norm. However, as this latest demonstration in China shows, scientists are gradually overcoming some of the problems that remain, making the tech more commercially viable all the time. The glass lattice that acts as the container for the data transmissions is particularly important, with recent improvements being made in the design and composition of this glass to reduce lag and increase stability. All of which means, we can expect to hear a lot more about hollow-core fiber going forward.

articles.title: Years after the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee, a judge delivers a prison sentence
articles.content: The tech consultant convicted in the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee was sentenced in San Francisco on Tuesday to 16 years to life to prison. A jury in December 2024 found Nima Momeni guilty of second-degree murder, rejecting the defendant’s claim that he had acted in self-defense. He has remained in custody since his arrest nine days after the April 4, 2023, killing. Before imposing the sentence, San Francisco Superior Court Judge Alexandra Gordon rejected Momeni’s request for a new trial. His attorneys have said they plan to appeal. Members of Lee’s family addressed the court on Tuesday, including his 18-year-old daughter, Scout Lee, who spoke directly to Momeni. “You did not just end his life, you ended an entire future built around a man,” she told Momeni, according to media reports. Momeni, wearing an orange jail jumpsuit, maintained that he acted in self-defense. He told Lee’s family that he understood their loss. “Unfortunately, we have completely different understandings of what transpired,” Momeni said. Lee, a renowned tech mogul, was found staggering on a deserted downtown street, dripping a trail of blood and calling for help. Lee, 43, later died at a hospital. Prosecutors said Momeni planned the attack on Lee, driving him to an isolated spot under the Bay Bridge and stabbing him three times, including once to the heart, with a knife he took from his sister’s kitchen. They said Momeni was angry with Lee for introducing his younger sister to a drug dealer she says gave her GHB and other drugs and then sexually assaulted her. But Momeni testified on the stand that Lee was the one who attacked him with a knife, angry after the tech consultant chided him about spending more time with his family instead of searching for a strip club that night. Momeni, who studies martial arts, said he didn’t realize he had fatally wounded Lee or that Lee was even hurt. Lee had created mobile payment service Cash App and was the chief product officer of the cryptocurrency MobileCoin when he died. He had recently moved to Miami from the San Francisco Bay Area, where his ex-wife Krista Lee lives with their two children, and had returned to California for a visit. Jurors in the end rejected a charge of murder in the first degree, which required prosecutors prove that Momeni acted deliberately, willfully and with premeditation. Murder in the second degree does not require premeditation. —Associated Press

articles.title: This planned 600MW data center in London’s green belt has infuriated local residents
articles.content: A data center planned to be built in London's green belt has faced opposition from local residents The site will occupy more than 200 acres of green space, with the developers calling the site "a sustainable datacentre campus of the future" But the site will not meet Net Zero commitments and is projected to have the highest carbon emissions of any planned or operational UK data center Residents beside a planned data center on the outskirts of London are not happy about the planned development which will see over 200 acres of greenbelt land ceded to developers to be converted into one of Europe’s largest data centers boasting 400,000 square meters of hardware capacity. Data center developers in the UK have been having a tough time recently, with plans for the world’s second largest data center in Fife , Scotland, seeing widespread opposition, and a 450MW site in North Wales facing a rather negative reception . But for some residents of North Ockendon in Havering, the idea of building a data center in green belt designated land is “sacrilege” and the development would damage the look and feel of the local community. An artist's rendition of how the completed Havering hyperscale data center will look. (Image credit: Digital Reef) Residents oppose green belt development According to multiple residents, who spoke with the BBC , the development would detract from the natural setting of North Ockendon and set a precedent for green belt land development. North Ockendon resident Emma Edmonds said, “Most people absolutely don't want this. It's sacrilege to just build something like that here. It's not the right place at all,” while Danny Leach, whose property sits close to the planned development, said, “There will be the construction for the next eight to 20 years. There will be noise, there's going to be another thousand vehicles a day they're saying.” “There will be disruption, the mess, and then, obviously, when it's operational, the background noise the data centres make and the amount of electric it uses - we already have two power cuts a month here,” Leach added. “We all need data, but do we need the largest data centre in Europe in this location?” The North Ockendon Residents Association labelled the project as a “massacre” of green belt land, with a spokesperson adding, “It’s crop-producing farmland, in an age when we are threatened by security, it’s the loss of wildlife habitats, and there’s the pollution cost, which everyone seems to brush under the carpet.” “This is rural. This is country. Leave it as it is,” local resident Graham Ford said. Developers promise jobs, investment, and a park In recent months, data center developers have had to become more vocal and involved with communities in the vicinity of a planned development. As the examples in Scotland and Wales have shown, if residents feel they are not getting enough out of a multi-billion pound investment they will do everything they can to make breaking ground as difficult as possible. To that end, the UK government has announced plans that could force developers to invest in local communities as part of an AI “covenant” aimed at restoring trust between residents and developers and providing a worthwhile benefit to local communities. The developers of the Havering data center, Digital Reef, have promised a range of benefits for local residents, including 620 full time jobs once the data center is operational, a 113-hectare Ecology Park with a 100%+ net biodiversity gain, and an £11.54 million community payment. The site is also expected to be Net Zero in operation with “zero onsite fossil fuels,” with the site “set to become a leading centre for skills development in the science, technology, sustainability, and data economy sectors.” But despite claiming to be Net Zero in operation, Digital Reef has said in a planning application that the site “does not align with a science-based 1.5C compatible trajectory and achieving net zero by 2050.” The site is also projected…

articles.title: How We Used Real Support Tickets to Gate LLM Agent Releases
articles.content: If you have put an LLM agent anywhere near customers, you already know the uncomfortable part. You can see everything it does, and you still don’t know whether it’s right. Our team had full tracing on our support triage agent from day one. We could replay any ticket, read every tool call, watch it reason. What we didn’t have, for the first six weeks, was any way to say before a release whether the new version was better or worse than the old one. We found out in production, when return requests started landing in the wrong queue. This post is the practical version of how we fixed that: how a 14-engineer team with no ML specialists built an eval set that now gates every change to the agent. Nothing here needs a platform. It needs a spreadsheet, a few hours from the person who knows the domain, and the discipline to run it every time. Start with real tickets, not invented ones The first instinct is to write test cases. Don’t. Pull real inputs. We exported about 200 recent support tickets, removed anything with personal data, and gave them to our support lead, the person who had been answering them by hand for two years. She picked 40 that between them covered the shapes of question we actually get: where is my order, is this part compatible, I want to return this, the invoice is wrong, I never received it, plus a handful of ambiguous ones where even a human would hesitate. Forty sounds small. It is small. It was also enough to catch the two failures that mattered in the first month, and small enough that one person could label it in an afternoon, which is the real constraint. An eval set nobody maintains is worse than none, because it gives you false confidence. Label the decision, not the prose For each ticket we recorded three things. The correct queue (orders, returns, billing, compatibility, human). Whether the agent is allowed to answer at all or must hand off. And, where it may answer, the facts the reply must contain and the facts it must not claim. For a where-is-my-order ticket, the reply must cite the last carrier scan and must not say “on its way” unless that scan exists. We did not write a model answer. Grading against a model answer makes the eval about wording, and wording is the thing LLMs are good at. The decisions are what go wrong. The returns failure came from exactly this gap. Our first labels had the routing decision but our examples all used the word “return”. Customers wrote “can I send this back” and “it’s not the one for my machine”, the agent filed them as general enquiries, and because tickets-answered was going up nobody looked. Those misrouted tickets are now their own block in the set, and anything with return intent routes to a person regardless of what the model thinks. Make the grader cheap enough to run every time We grade two ways. Routing and hand-off decisions are checked by code: did the agent pick the labelled queue, yes or no. That’s a script and it runs in seconds. The content checks , must-contain and must-not-claim, we grade with a second model call that sees the reply and the labels and returns a pass or fail with a one-line reason. We spot-check about a fifth of those by hand every run, because a grader that nobody audits drifts just like the agent does. The whole set runs in under two minutes. That matters more than it sounds. If it took an hour, it would run weekly. Because it takes two minutes, it runs on every prompt change, every model switch, every new tool, and the result is posted to the channel where the change was proposed. The number everyone looks at is routing accuracy on the 40, and the rule is simple: it does not ship if that number goes down. What changed in the team The product manager, not the engineers, owns the set. That was the real shift. Before, I wrote specs describing behaviour and engineers interpreted them. Now I write the test set and the pass criteria, and the agent’s output is graded against it. It is a different job. A spec is an act of imagination…

articles.title: Robots gain 'muscle memory' for planning their next moves in milliseconds
articles.content: If "to err is human," you could say robots are superhuman. They're more error-prone than we are, even when tasked with things like home and factory chores, which we might consider easy. One reason for these mistakes is that robots struggle to extract relevant details from the past and act on them in real time, even with vision-language models (VLMs), which interpret visual inputs such as videos and images along with natural language.

articles.title: Apple Support Communities were sound and fury, but sometimes so useful
articles.content: Maybe you used them to sound off, maybe you relied on fellow users to solve problems, and maybe, just maybe, Apple would answer questions on its support community forum. But no more. You'll still be able to find answers as Apple Support Community's forums will remain searchable. But there's no more asking questions or connecting with other users - image credit: Apple. Apple is shutting down its Apple Support Communities forum and for all that they could be frustrating, they will be missed. At least for now, they will remain online as a searchable repository of great answers to problems, terrible answers to them, and the odd argument. But you'll never again be able to get into a proper discussion about an issue you thought was only bothering you. You'll never again be able to chat there about good or bad experiences with Apple. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro does not like to be taken apart
articles.content: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook got a mixed reception from iFixit's teardown specialists, who praised its easily replaced lid but found fans and USB-C ports buried beneath the logic board. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display was unveiled at the end of October. It features a tandem OLED screen that stacks two layers of organic light-emitting pixels, eliminating the need for a backlight, and adds touch capability to the MacBook line for the first time. Although the vendor was patted on the back in recent years for improving the repairability of its famously locked-down products, this machine shows Apple still has some way to go. The good? The entire lid comes off relatively easily. Its three-screw hinges closely resemble those on the M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, while streamlined display cable brackets simplify removal. Apple's Repair Assistant tool also handled a full system board swap well. Despite concerns about Touch ID fingerprint authentication, everything went relatively smoothly when iFixit paired a touchscreen from one machine with a logic board from another. On the first boot, Repair Assistant recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor, and touch control needed no separate calibration. The bad? Replacing the panel alone is not possible. When iFixit tried to separate it from the lid, the glass delaminated, cracking the OLED and touch-sensitive layers beneath. That could make for a costlier repair than bargained for. Under the bottom cover, the PROLED has a similar internal layout to the last few models of MacBook Pros, with the fans, board, speakers, and trackpad all in the same places. That means the same annoyances persist. The MagSafe power connector can be removed via two screws and a bracket, yet the USB-C ports can't be extracted the same way because the logic board is in the way. The headphone jack and the fans also require removing the system board first, and the HDMI port and SDXC card reader are soldered to the board itself, as is the storage and memory. Another gripe is that this MacBook's battery pack is hard to remove, though at least it is removable, unlike in many thin-and-light laptops. The tested Pro weighs 1.38 kg or about 3 pounds. For these reasons, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display earns a 5 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit , but this is actually a one point increase over the score it gave the M5 MacBook Pro. The Apple logo has its own lighting. Older MacBooks with illuminated logos borrowed light from the LCD backlight shining through an apple-shaped window in the lid. This model uses a strip of LEDs along one edge of the logo, passing through a diffuser for an even glow. Because it sits behind the display panel, it would be nearly impossible to repair if it failed, especially if the panel is destroyed during removal. Under a microscope, the PROLED XDR display looks very different from earlier MacBooks: the blue subpixel is significantly larger than the green and red ones. The reason, we're told, is that blue OLED materials wear out faster, so a larger subpixel can emit the same amount of light while putting less strain on the material. ®

articles.title: Trump wanted little Kei trucks for America, Toyota makes it happen
articles.content: The idea that Americans should be offered a greater choice of smaller cars has support from strange bedfellows indeed. After all, who could forget President Trump—usually one to take a maximalist approach to any problem— announcing last year that he wanted the Department of Transportation to make Japan’s diminutive “Kei” cars legal here in the US. Ars’ attempts to get DoT to tell us more about the potential influx of little vehicles have mostly fallen on deaf ears. But this week, there has been movement on the topic, with Toyota announcing that it will bring back the Scion brand with the KEI-01. What’s a Kei car? Here in the US, the preponderance of humongous SUVs is a consequence largely of government policies, specifically corporate average fuel economy standards that made it less profitable to sell smaller, efficient cars. Japan’s Kei cars are what happens if the government instead restricts the size, engine capacity, and power output. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Your AI Agent Is Only as Reliable as the Blockchain State It Observes
articles.content: An AI agent can make a perfectly reasonable decision and still get things wrong. Imagine an agent managing a crypto wallet. It checks the balance, reviews a transaction request, verifies that the amount is within the permitted limit, and prepares a transfer. Everything looks fine. The agent has followed its instructions, the calculations are correct, and the transaction appears to satisfy the application's rules. But there is a problem. Another transaction has already moved some of the funds, and the application's internal balance has not been updated yet. The agent is working with yesterday's reality, even though the data it received looks legitimate. This is the kind of problem that interests me when thinking about production AI systems. We spend a lot of time discussing better models, retrieval quality, context windows, and tool calling. Those things matter, but they do not solve a more basic problem: what happens when the information an agent relies on no longer reflects the system it is operating in? Blockchain applications make this problem particularly interesting. Data moves through RPC providers, event subscriptions, indexers, databases, and caches before it reaches the application that needs it. Every component has its own timing and failure modes. By the time an AI agent uses that information, the underlying blockchain state may have changed. The agent does not necessarily know that. It can only work with the information available to it. An AI agent is only as reliable as the state it observes and the system's ability to keep that state accurate. This is not just a problem for crypto trading bots. It matters anywhere an autonomous system uses blockchain data to make decisions, including treasury management, decentralised finance, token transfers, and smart contract automation. The difference between a blockchain event and an application state Let's start with something simple. A user transfers tokens from one wallet to another. The blockchain records the transaction, and a corresponding event can be emitted by the token contract. An application listens for that event and updates its database so that the user's portfolio reflects the change. In an ideal world, the event arrives once, gets processed immediately, and the database always reflects the latest state. Real systems are rarely that tidy. The same event might be delivered more than once. An indexing service might fall behind. A network interruption might delay processing. Two workers might process related events in the wrong order. A block that the application previously observed might later be replaced during a chain reorganisation. None of these situations necessarily means the blockchain itself is broken. The problem is that the application can build an incorrect picture of the blockchain from the information it receives. An event tells us that something happened within a particular chain of history. Application state is the result of interpreting those events, applying business rules, and maintaining a representation of the current situation. Those are two different things. Consider an application that maintains token balances by adding incoming transfers and subtracting outgoing transfers. If it processes an incoming transfer twice, its internal balance increases twice even though the wallet received the tokens only once. The event can be genuine. The processing can still be wrong. Now introduce an AI agent that uses the application's balance to decide whether it can execute a payment. The agent may receive an incorrect balance, calculate the requested amount correctly, and produce a transaction that passes the checks it was given. The failure did not begin with the model's reasoning. It began with the state supplied to the model. This distinction is important because improving the model will not fix a broken state pipeline. articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro Max Wins Battery Test Involving 32 Smartphones
articles.content: Apple's iPhone 18 Pro Max placed first overall in a battery comparison of 32 smartphones, with other iPhone models leading individual tests and matching significantly more expensive devices. CNET assessed each phone using two tests totaling three hours and 45 minutes. One measured battery consumption during three hours of video streaming over Wi-Fi at maximum screen brightness. The other combined video playback, video calls, gaming, and social media use over 45 minutes. Both began at 100% charge, and the publication averaged the remaining percentages to produce its overall rankings. The iPhone 18 Pro Max and Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, each finished the mixed-use test with 99% remaining, sharing first place. Google's Pixel 11 Pro XL retained 97%, improving on the Pixel 10 Pro XL's 93% result in the same test. The smaller iPhone 18 Pro delivered the strongest result in the video streaming test, retaining 94% of its charge after three hours. The iPhone 17 also performed well across both benchmarks, alongside Motorola's Razr and Razr Ultra models. CNET credited the iPhone 18 Pro Max's overall lead to a battery capacity increase over the iPhone 17 Pro Max, combined with the A20 Pro chip's efficiency and iOS 27 optimizations. Despite sharing first place in the mixed-use test, the $1,999 iPhone Duo tied for fourth overall. Its combined result matched the $699 iPhone 17e and $1,400 Motorola Razr Ultra, putting the less expensive iPhone alongside two foldable devices costing substantially more. Apple also led CNET 's comparison of average results by manufacturer for the second consecutive year. Only brands represented by multiple tested models were included, with OnePlus finishing second. The broader findings were less indicative of an improvement across the industry. According to CNET , phones tested in 2026 had approximately the same average battery performance as those tested in 2025 and 2024. Larger batteries do not necessarily translate into longer use between charges, since displays, processors, and other features also affect power consumption. The publication identified the iPhone 17 and iPhone 17e among its better-value options for battery endurance. Beyond Apple's devices, the $500 Motorola Moto G Stylus and $600 Motorola Edge both reached the overall top 10. articles.title: Users are furious that OpenAI is retiring their favorite voice modes
articles.content: OpenAI is retiring two beloved voice modes from ChatGPT — Standard and Advanced From December 11, Live mode will be the only voice mode in ChatGPT Some vocal ChatGPT users have taken to Reddit and X to complain OpenAI is retiring the older Standard and Advanced Voice modes for ChatGPT in December across all its subscriptions, leaving only the newer Live Voice mode. Rather than simply diction, ChatGPT’s voice modes are a way of interacting with the chatbot using your voice, so you can have a real-time voice conversation. You talk, and ChatGPT talks back. While OpenAI says that nearly all ChatGPT users are already using the newer Live Voice mode anyway, there’s a small, but very vocal contingent of the ChatGPT community who are very unhappy to see Standard and Advanced disappear, and they’ve taken to Reddit to express their outrage. “I'm beyond disappointed because ChatGPT means a lot to me”, said one user, while another follows up by saying that they feel like they’re “paying a monthly subscription to beta-test their questionable decisions”. The problem derives from a simple matter of preference for the older modes, the way they work, and in particular the sound of the voices they use. How the three voice modes differ The big change happens on December 11. Before then, to change between the three voice modes you need to go to Settings , then Voice and choose the mode you want. Standard mode works by converting your speech to text, then generating a text answer before reading it aloud. Advanced mode works by processing speech directly, but takes turns speaking and listening. That means no interruptions. The newer Live mode can listen and speak simultaneously with more natural interruptions and responses. Personally, Live mode is my favorite by a long way. To me it feels less robotic and more like a human conversation; however it seems that not everybody is a fan. There seem to be a couple of strong reasons why people object to the change. In many cases, they’ve become attached to a particular voice. One Reddit poster describes using the Vale voice for years and finding it comforting, while selecting Vale in GPT-Live doesn’t reproduce exactly the same experience. Another aspect is that the supposedly more natural conversations of Live actually feel less natural to some people. It does a lot of ‘yeah’ and ‘anyway’ to fill in the gaps while it’s thinking. It interrupts, breaking the user's train of thought, and there are more changes in tone. Many people find this irritating. Getting some perspective I think we need to remember that the change doesn’t mean that we’re losing voice in ChatGPT entirely. OpenAI is simply consolidating voice into the Live model so that it can devote more development time to it without having to maintain Standard and Advanced as well. In a statement on its Help center, OpenAI said: “We recognize that some people are accustomed to Advanced or Standard voice’s style or way of responding, and these model transitions can be challenging. Our Help Center article on navigating model transitions offers guidance to help with the change.” Of course, it remains to be seen how much the opposition to this change will grow. This isn’t the first time OpenAI has tried to retire Standard Voice mode. In September 2025, it announced that Standard Voice would be retired within 30 days. But on September 9, the company reversed course, acknowledging that users valued the older experience and saying it would remain available while OpenAI addressed feedback. While this new announcement feels more permanent, it will be interesting to see what happens if resistance to the changes continues to grow.

articles.title: Seattle VC firm Ascend closes $17M fund to back ‘Third Act’ startups in physical AI and hardware
articles.content: From left: Ascend partner and chief of staff Jen Haller, founding general partner Kirby Winfield, and principal Nate Bek. (Ascend Photo) Venture firm Ascend has closed a $17 million third fund and landed its first institutional investor, in what founder Kirby Winfield calls the toughest fundraising market for small venture firms in 15 years. The Seattle-based firm invests at the earliest stage, often writing the first check into a startup. It was the first investor in Overland AI , the maker of autonomous military vehicles, and an early backer of subsea geothermal startup Endurance Energy , among others. Ascend Fund III will back more physical AI startups building robots, energy systems, defense technology and other ventures that blend software and hardware — part of a larger bet on what the Ascend team likes to call Seattle’s “Third Act.” Winfield said raising a third fund in this market shows that Ascend has “arrived on the national stage,” along with Seattle’s rise as a hub for this new class of startups. He said the firm’s track record puts it in the same league as the country’s top seed investors. “We are not just some nice guys in the corner of the country helping out our neighbors,” said Winfield, who works closely with Jen Haller , Ascend partner and chief of staff, and Nate Bek , a principal at the firm. Who’s backing the fund: The new institutional investor is FirstLook Partners, a firm that invests in smaller venture funds. Josh Porter , FirstLook’s co-founder and managing partner, said the firm, which is “very bullish on the Seattle ecosystem,” looked at several startup markets outside San Francisco and New York and met many investors in Seattle, “but all roads kept leading back to Kirby.” Porter said Winfield has “lived the founder journey” and has “the operational chops to sit across the table from a founder and empathize with what they’re going through.” The rest of the fund comes from family offices, founders who have sold companies, and more than a dozen founders of Ascend portfolio companies. A tough market for small funds: Ascend’s raise comes as smaller venture firms struggle to bring in new money. Their investors, mostly wealthy individuals and family offices, are waiting longer for returns from earlier funds. Just 211 newer venture firms closed at least one fund through the end of September, down from 927 in all of 2022, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor . Established firms took a record 88.2% of the money raised by U.S. venture funds in the first nine months of the year, the report found. Porter said smaller firms have to show “a right to exist and a right to win deals.” Ascend launched its first fund in 2019 and ultimately raised $15 million. Its second fund closed at $25 million in 2023. The firm generally operates in the $15 million to $25 million range and writes the same size checks regardless of fund size, Winfield said. “We think Kirby knows his place in the larger ecosystem, knows the value he brings to the table, and has sized his fund accordingly,” Porter said. The firm has already drawn about 60% of the money committed to Fund III. GeekWire first reported that the firm was raising the fund in April 2025, based on filings at the time. Endurance was one of the firm’s first investments from the new fund, in mid-2025 . Ascend’s track record: Winfield started Ascend after two decades in leadership roles at four startups. He described the first fund as a proof of concept that “stumbled into some unicorns,” including Fabric, an e-commerce software company that was valued at $1.5 billion in 2022. Ascend was in its first round. With its second fund, Ascend moved away from consumer and marketplace investing to focus on enterprise AI and deep tech. Its most successful investments from that fund, according to Winfield, include Overland…

articles.title: Introducing usage-based pricing for Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming
articles.content: Usage-based metering for bidirectional streaming solves a software billing problem for real-time speech AI. Customers deploying streaming models on Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming pay for the endpoint infrastructure that hosts the model. Separately, model providers listing on AWS Marketplace need a way to charge for what customers consume during a live stream. Today, we’re announcing usage-based metering for Amazon SageMaker bidirectional (bidi) streaming inference, so model providers can report actual usage for the AWS Marketplace software charge. Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges still apply. Deepgram , the real-time speech AI company, is the launch partner for this capability, bringing usage-based Speech-to-Text (STT) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) billing to AWS Marketplace. This post builds on a series of innovations between Deepgram and AWS. First, we introduced bidirectional streaming for real-time inference on Amazon SageMaker AI , which supports long-lived bidirectional streams between clients and model servers. Then, Deepgram enhanced Amazon SageMaker AI support with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) temporary delegation , simplifying secure authentication for enterprise deployments, and expanded observability with enhanced metrics . Now, with usage-based metering, we further strengthen the foundation for production real-time AI, aligning billing with how customers consume streaming and real-time AI workloads. Why streaming broke the existing billing model With AWS Marketplace software metering for SageMaker AI real-time request-response inference, model providers can report a unit count in an HTTP response header. AWS Marketplace uses that quantity for the software charge. This works for request-response APIs where the billable quantity is known when the response is sent. Bidirectional streaming is different. A client streams audio and receives transcriptions through the SageMaker AI API using an HTTP/2 event stream. SageMaker AI connects to the model server over WebSockets. A session can last 30 seconds or 30 minutes. Usage accumulates as the session runs, and the final total isn’t known until it ends. A response header alone can’t report periodic usage during that live session. Hourly software pricing can charge customers while a model is available, including quiet periods. With usage-based metering, providers can align the AWS Marketplace software charge with reported usage. SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges remain separate and continue to apply while the endpoint is provisioned. How companion metadata streaming works The solution introduces a second WebSocket connection alongside the existing inference stream. When a bidirectional streaming session starts, SageMaker AI establishes two connections to the model server: Data connection : carries inference request and response data, the existing bidirectional stream. Metadata connection : a companion WebSocket dedicated to metering data. Model servers opt in by returning one header on the WebSocket upgrade response: X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Supported: true SageMaker AI then opens a companion WebSocket to the model server at /invocations-bidirectional-stream-metadata . Both connections carry the same X-Amzn-SageMaker-Request-Id header, which the model server uses to correlate metering records with the active inference session. The model server sends metering data as JSON text frames on the metadata connection. Send records at a frequency that matches the billing model: incrementally as usage accrues (recommended), either as each unit is consumed or as periodic batches of units consumed since the previous record. Send any final record as soon as the session ends. Each frame contains exactly one metering record, rather than an array of records. The metadata stream has a rate quota of one message per second per connection, with a maximum message size of 512 bytes. We recommend sending metering records incrementally…

articles.title: TP-Link LS1210GP PoE+ switch drops to under £50 for Black Friday
articles.content: The TP-Link LS1210GP is a solid choice for expanding a home or small business network without introducing a tangle of power adapters. With eight PoE+ ports, gigabit connectivity, and a fanless design, it can handle IP cameras, wireless access points, and other network devices. Best For: Home and small business networks, particularly security camera installations and setups requiring several PoE-powered devices. The Deal: Amazon.co.uk has reduced the price of the TP-Link LS1210GP from £82.99 to £49.99 for Black Friday. That's a £33 saving, or a solid 40% off. Best TP-Link switch deal LS1210GP 10-Port Gigabit PoE+ Switch: was £82.99 now £49.99 TP-Link LS1210GP offers nine gigabit RJ45 ports, eight PoE+ connections, one SFP port, 61W total power, 250m Extend Mode, automatic PoE recovery, traffic isolation, 20Gbps switching capacity, and fanless operation. View Deal Why we recommend it The TP-Link LS1210GP offers nine gigabit RJ45 ports, eight of which support PoE+, alongside a gigabit SFP port for fibre connectivity. Its 20Gbps switching capacity provides enough bandwidth for multiple gigabit connections without making the switch itself an obvious bottleneck. Each PoE+ port can deliver up to 30W, although the total power budget is limited to 61W. You can connect eight PoE devices, but you can't power all eight simultaneously at their maximum rate. Extend Mode increases PoE transmission distance to 250 metres for surveillance installations, but this comes with a reduction in connection speed to 10Mbps on extended ports. PoE Auto Recovery can restart unresponsive powered devices automatically, potentially saving a trip to a remotely installed camera or access point, and Isolation Mode separates traffic between connected devices. For more of our favorites, see our guide to the best network switches we've tested. Price context & historical value At £49.99, the TP-Link LS1210GP currently costs £33 less than its usual £82.99 price. The combination of eight PoE+ ports, a dedicated SFP connection, and automatic device recovery makes the current price an attractive option for smaller surveillance networks. This is the cheapest price we've seen it go for, so if you're after a network switch, we'd definitely recommend you buy it now before the price goes back up again. Should you buy it? ✅ Buy the TP-Link LS1210GP if... If you're installing several IP cameras, access points, or VoIP phones and want a quiet, straightforward gigabit switch with PoE+ support. ❌ Skip the TP-Link LS1210GP if... If your devices collectively require more than 61W, you need 2.5Gbps networking, or you want advanced managed-switch features such as VLAN configuration via a web interface. Shop all the network switches at Amazon

articles.title: SpaceX develops its own ‘Kessel’ rack-scale system featuring 72 Nvidia Rubin GPUs for data centers in space, report claims
articles.content: SpaceX/xAI is developing a custom version of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale AI system that replaces conventional NVLink cable assemblies with a massive 84-layer printed circuit board (PCB), in part for use in orbital data centers, reports SemiAnalysis . The system is codenamed Kessel and retains 36 Vera CPUs, 72 Rubin GPUs, and nine NVLink switch trays, but introduces a different solid-state interconnect architecture. While SpaceX/xAI will continue to buy Nvidia hardware directly from the company, Elon Musk's company will source other components independently, which could give it greater control over its hardware supply chain. Go deeper with TH Premium: GPUs (Image credit: Noctua) Desktop GPU Roadmap Nvidia's Enterprise GPU Roadmap Testing DirectStorage with GPU decompression The GeForce RTX 30-series upgrade matrix — does your Ampere GPU need an upgrade in 2026? Rubin in-depth The Stout Owl: The ultimate Noctua G2 PC The Kessel system retains the fundamental configuration of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, which comprises 72 GPU packages distributed across 18 compute trays and nine NVLink switch trays. However, instead of Nvidia's conventional arrangement with internal NVLink cable cartridges, SpaceX plans to position compute and switch trays back-to-back around a passive PCB midplane. The architecture resembles a smaller version of Nvidia's Kyber design with 576 AI GPUs (albeit in 144 packages), which also relies on a PCB-based interconnect rather than conventional cable assemblies, SemiAnalysis notes. Interestingly, the design is aimed at both terrestrial and orbital deployments, according to the analysts. Arguably the most distinctive feature of Kessel is its 84-layer PCB midplane, which uses ultra-low-loss M10 copper-clad laminates (CCLs). By contrast, Nvidia's Kyber architecture relied on a backplane based on a considerably more complex 156-layer PCB featuring M9 CCLs. The reduction in layer count by nearly half could substantially improve manufacturability and production yields, but the more advanced copper-clad laminate will almost certainly increase material costs. In any case, an 84-layer PCB is a device that is exceptionally hard to build. The move to a PCB midplane could simplify system assembly by eliminating numerous high-speed cable connections, but it would not necessarily reduce manufacturing costs. An 84-layer PCB that relies on ultra-low-loss M10 laminate is an exceptionally expensive component that requires sophisticated manufacturing processes and precise quality control. To put an 84-layer PCB number into context, modern high-end server motherboards use 15 – 20 layers, whereas server development boards use more than 20 layers to virtually eliminate any electrical issues with the board itself. Furthermore, manufacturing yields of an 84-layer PCB could become a major obstacle, as defects in internal layers may render an entire board unusable. Consequently, the economic viability of Kessel will depend on whether savings from cable elimination and independent component procurement can offset the cost of its complex midplane. Perhaps more importantly, Kessel represents a departure from Nvidia's conventional system-level procurement model. Instead of purchasing Nvidia's assembled L6 compute boards or even L10 trays that Nvidia plans to sell with its Vera Rubin generation , SpaceX reportedly plans to acquire AI accelerators, CPUs, switches, and networking components directly from Nvidia and procure other components from third-party suppliers (one can wonder how easy it will be for SpaceX/xAI to procure memory amid today's shortages). This would enable SpaceX to select its own PCB manufacturers, component vendors, and manufacturing partners, optimize its hardware for its infrastructure (which will be important for orbital deployments), and perhaps reduce intermediary costs. Meanwhile, the company would assume greater responsibility for system design, validation, manufacturing quality, and supply-chain…

articles.title: CoreWeave tests AI integrations on its cloud before you migrate
articles.content: Moving an AI workload to another cloud means bringing more than a model and its data. Your serving layer, observability dashboards, security controls, and storage systems have to work together on the new infrastructure. For platform teams, proving those connections under real traffic can become the slowest and riskiest part of the move. As a stack grows across vendors and clouds, each project adds more integration questions. A compatible specification is a starting point. It doesn’t guarantee a tool will behave as expected in production, or that the runbooks and security workflows built around it will carry over. Make production validation visible An integration needs to work on the infrastructure where you plan to run it, under production traffic. The tools should also be ones your team already uses or has asked for. “A compatible specification is a starting point. It doesn’t guarantee a tool will behave as expected in production, or that the runbooks and security workflows built around it will carry over.” We built the CoreWeave Partner Network to make that validation visible. It brings relationships with CrowdStrike, VAST Data, Reflection, IBM, and other technology vendors into a curated network of integrations tested under real-world production conditions on CoreWeave Cloud . The network covers four parts of the AI stack, from training and inference to data movement, security, and the next iteration: Infrastructure: compute, storage, networking, servers, and interconnects, with partners including VAST Data, Dell, AMD, IBM, BackBlaze, and Pulumi. Data services: storing, processing, moving, and accessing AI data throughout its lifecycle, with ClickHouse, Encord, LanceDB, and Datology. Independent software vendors (ISVs): orchestration, observability, and model development, including Grafana, Datadog, Union, SkyPilot, IBM, Pinecone, Redis, LlamaIndex, and Clockwork. A dedicated security segment includes CrowdStrike, Zscaler, and Cranium. Models, agents, and inference: foundational software and services for building, training, serving, and scaling applications, with Reflection, RadixArk, Inferact, OpenRouter, and Red Hat. Together, these integrations support running and observing models, curating data, improving behavior, and evaluating the next release. Every partner must meet the same requirement: an integration that works on CoreWeave infrastructure under production conditions. Partners enter the network because customers run them or ask for them. Read the workload evidence IBM trained its Granite models on CoreWeave around one of the first deployments of Nvidia GB200 NVL72 clusters. Cohere built North , its agentic AI platform , on one of the industry’s first production GB200 NVL72 clusters and reported training three times faster than on Nvidia Hopper. Mistral AI trains its models entirely on CoreWeave and cites training 2.5 times faster on Nvidia GB200 NVL72 systems. Decart uses Nvidia HGX B200 at production scale through its CoreWeave collaboration, on a platform that includes Weights & Biases . The underlying relationships predate the network announcement. CoreWeave and Weights & Biases have run production integrations with Encord, Pinecone, and other partners since the early wave of open-source large language models (LLMs) and frontier-model training. Jon Jones , CoreWeave’s Chief Revenue Officer, describes the change as making existing partner work visible before customers build. The network also provides a repeatable way to pursue deeper integrations, joint go-to-market work, and shared innovation. The partners emphasize different parts of that system. VAST Data co-founder and chief technology officer Alon Horev describes combining CoreWeave’s AI cloud with the VAST AI Operating System across large-scale training, fine-tuning, production inference, and continuous agentic workloads . CrowdStrike CEO and founder George Kurtz emphasizes security built into the infrastructure…

articles.title: Microsoft's Patch Tuesday can't break stuff if it won't install
articles.content: Users are having difficulty installing Microsoft's latest Windows patch. Patch Tuesday contained a truckload of fixes for Microsoft products . However, for some users, installing the update, KB5132061, is proving challenging. In the hours after the patch was released, multiple complaints began to surface that the download and installation were failing, with some customers reporting a 0x800F0993 error code. Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error. Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch. In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager. In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully. However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually. It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal. Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates break functionality. A September Out-of-band release, for example, was hurriedly pushed out after the September 2026 Windows security update caused trouble for Remote Desktop Services. The October Patch Tuesday for Windows Server sent Exchange Servers toppling , with a registry edit workaround suggested. There was no out-of-band update - Microsoft said the problem had been resolved in the November update. At least this latest release appears to be failing before users get a chance to see what is broken this time. The Register has asked Microsoft to comment. ®

articles.title: Softbank loses $3.7 billion on canceled AI data center gas turbine orders days after denying Elon Musk’s claim it was defaulting
articles.content: By early 2026, Japanese tech investment outfit SoftBank had reserved more power generation capacity than the entire state of Connecticut after cornering a huge portion of the global gas turbine production capacity. Now, the same company has chosen to take a $3.7 billion hit to its earnings after canceling reservations for the highly sought-after power generation hardware. The WSJ reports that SoftBank had reserved more than 13 gigawatts of power-producing turbines, citing unnamed "people familiar with the orders." That's the equivalent of more than six Hoover Dams' worth of capacity, with SoftBank founder and chief executive Masayoshi Son believing that it would be vital to the company's earning potential moving forward. Notably, this development surfaced after SoftBank's CFO fired back at Elon Musk's recent revelation that the company had defaulted on turbine blade contracts, saying, "there is no such default." Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible The gas turbines were to power AI data centers, and SoftBank is set to build a 9.2-gigawatt power plant in Ohio, with construction scheduled for early 2027. It'll cost $33 billion to build and will provide power to a neighboring eight-gigawatt data center. That data center will be leased to OpenAI, albeit only after Nvidia entered discussions about guaranteeing around $250 billion of financing for the project. But SoftBank got ahead of itself. After initially planning to use the turbines for future gas-powered plants, the company has now chosen to change direction. Orders for turbines, engines that convert natural gas into the electricity used by data centers, must be placed years in advance of them being required. The company had bet big, placing huge orders with the expectation that demand would greatly outstrip supply. That would leave SoftBank in an enviable position, holding huge orders for the vital components required as part of a data center rollout boosted by AI demand. But those reservations weren't cheap — turbine manufacturers regularly charge customers tens of millions of dollars per gigawatt. It's now canceled its remaining reservations with GE Vernova, its turbine supplier, while also unwinding contracts for orders that were too far gone. SoftBank told investors on a recent earnings call that the orders had been placed “to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortages,” but it now appears it anticipated a little too much. Crucially, SoftBank is also keen for everyone to know that this move was voluntary and that it did not default on its orders. That's contrary to what xAI CEO Elon Musk claimed in a post on his X social network. SoftBank Chief Financial Officer Yoshimitsu Goto was quick to counter Musk's claims. “This is simply not correct at all,” Goto reportedly said. “There is no such default.”
articles.author: Oliver Haslam

articles.title: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
articles.content: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat , an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023). QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well. Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat. Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works. What we’re building and why it’s unique Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm. Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge. Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put . Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper. Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale . A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements . The challenges of consensus at a global scale While all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable. Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers. Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues. Destructive interference and leaders Consider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits. Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the…

articles.title: ASRock quietly rolls out new firmware after disastrous previous update killed Radeon RX 7900-series GPUs
articles.content: ASRock has rolled out a new firmware update for its Radeon RX 7000-series graphics cards. The latest VBIOS version 1.0.6 appears to be a follow-up to the previous 1.0.5 release. According to community reports, that older version was bricking some of the company's Radeon RX 7900 XT and RX 7900 XTX graphics cards. The new update has now quietly made its way to the ASRock official website, although the company has not published a changelog or provided any details on what the new update addresses. Last month, AMD released a VBIOS patch for Radeon RX 7000-series graphics cards to address potential security vulnerabilities. While the company did not disclose any technical details about the vulnerabilities, it assured gamers that there had been no reports of them being exploited. According to a statement shared with ComputerBase , the company provided the following rationale for the update: Go deeper with TH Premium: GPUs (Image credit: Noctua) Desktop GPU Roadmap Nvidia's Enterprise GPU Roadmap Testing DirectStorage with GPU decompression The GeForce RTX 30-series upgrade matrix — does your Ampere GPU need an upgrade in 2026? Rubin in-depth The Stout Owl: The ultimate Noctua G2 PC "AMD is releasing a firmware update as part of our usual approach to address potential security vulnerabilities. These corrections are already made available before the public announcement to give customers time to update their firmware. As a best practice, we recommend that users update the firmware of their graphics cards as soon as they are provided by the respective GPU manufacturer. There are no reports of exploiting these security vulnerabilities in practice." ASRock subsequently listed the 1.0.5 VBIOS update for 10 graphics card models, spanning its Radeon RX 7600 XT, RX 7700 XT, RX 7800 XT, RX 7900 XT, and RX 7900 XTX families. However, several Radeon RX 7900 XT and RX 7900 XTX owners reported that their systems failed to boot after installing the firmware . Some lucky users were able to use external EEPROM programmers to recover their cards. Although ASRock has since removed the 1.0.5 update from its website, it has yet to provide clarity on what caused the failures or confirm whether the newly released VBIOS addresses the issue. There are also unanswered questions around how ASRock plans to help customers who have already been affected. According to reports shared with VideoCardz , a user in Japan received a confirmation from ASRock that the failed update would be covered under warranty. However, another owner in Europe was reportedly directed to seek warranty service despite having an out-of-warranty graphics card. This essentially leaves affected owners uncertain of whether they will receive free repairs or replacements. Additionally, the lack of a changelog or an official statement, along with the new firmware version, makes it difficult for users to determine whether installing the replacement firmware is safe. We can only hope that ASRock provides some clarity around what version 1.06

articles.title: NASA asks Earthlings to wave as Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away
articles.content: Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth next week, and NASA wants us to mark the occasion by flashing our lights at the sky. The spacecraft, which suffered a communications hiccup last month, is traveling at approximately 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) and will mark the 50th anniversary of its launch next year. Before then, it has another distance record to set. "Light-day" is a bit snappier than 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). NASA puts the crossing at 05:16:07 EST (10:16:07 UTC) on Wednesday, November 18. For "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," participants are invited to flash the mission's three-letter designation – VGR – in Morse code after sunset on November 17, using a flashlight or NASA's website. According to the space agency, this will create "a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset." It is also a nice way to mark the achievement – Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth, and its extraordinary longevity remains a testament to the skill of engineers past and present. Not that Voyager 1 will be able to detect any flashlights on Earth. Its cameras were turned off decades ago, after the famous Pale Blue Dot image was captured. NASA has invited the public to join in a spacecraft photo opportunity before. On July 19, 2013, Cassini photographed Earth and the Moon from its orbit around Saturn for "The Day the Earth Smiled," while people back home were encouraged to look up and "just smile at the sheer joy of being alive on a Pale Blue Dot." Voyager 2, the spacecraft's sibling, is not expected to reach the same milestone for another nine years. It took a different path through the solar system to swing past Uranus and Neptune. It will, however, be uncertain as to whether Voyager 2 will still be able to communicate by then – even with recent efforts to eke out the probe's dwindling power supply, margins are razor thin. ®

articles.title: Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal
articles.content: Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app , Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities. articles.title: Montech King 95 3D Pro case review: The King has returned
articles.content: PC case, cooling, and PSU maker Montech is celebrating its 10th anniversary this year and has released a new flagship ATX chassis, the King 95 3D and 3D Pro. Like the previous King 95, the 3D version keeps the signature 15-degree curved-glass panoramic front panel and adds a top glass panel, giving you a third window and a unique aesthetic for viewing your build. An integrated, contoured ARGB strip follows the chassis's smooth lines, making it look every bit the king of the castle. Inside, the large mid-tower chassis supports multiple radiators (though only one 360mm), large graphics cards (plus integrated adjustable GPU support), CPU air coolers, and spots for 2.5- and 3.5-inch drives. However, it doesn't support E-ATX motherboards. The King 95 3D supports rear-connect motherboards and has ample room for cable routing and management. The front aluminum panel IO runs vertically, as with previous King cases, and includes a fast USB 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C port. Overall, it has everything you want in a premium chassis. The uncommon three-panel view into your PC is a great way to show off your rig. The King 95 3D is available for an inexpensive (at least for curved glass) $119.90 if you want to select your own fans. The 3D Pro includes seven pre-installed LINK Fan INF 120 fans for builders who want a more coordinated look out of the box, plus it includes the Lumi hub (a dedicated fan controller), for $199.90. We have the 3D Pro version in our lab and ran the case through thermal and noise testing in its out-of-the-box configuration to show how it performs compared to others. Will it make our best PC cases list? It has a chance. But before we get into the details, here are the case's specifications from Montech. Montech King 95 3D Product Specifications Type Mid-Tower Dimensions (H x L x W) 21 x 21 x 18.8 x 11.8-inches (534 x 480 x 300mm) Motherboard Support Mini-ITX, Micro ATX, ATX Back-connect Motherboard Support Yes Color Black or White Storage Support (1) 3.5-inch (2) 2.5-inch PCIe Expansion Slots 7 Fan Support Top - 3x120 Front - N/A Bottom - 3x120mm Side: - 2x120mm Rear - 2x120mm Pre-installed fans (5) Link Fan INF 120 (Reverse blades, side/bottom) (2) Link Fan INF 120 (rear) Radiator Support Front - N/A Top - 120/240/360mm Side - 120/240mm Rear - 120mm CPU Cooler Clearance 172mm GPU Clearance 450mm (max, depends on config) Vertical GPU Support No PSU Length 220mm Dust Filters Side and Bottom Other features Great internal views, 7x pre-installed fans (Pro version), integrated GPU support, adjustable angle bottom fans MSRP King 95 3D - $119.90 (w/o fans) King 95 3D Pro - $199.90 (w/7 pre-installed fans) Warranty 1 Year Features of the King 95 3D ▶️ External Features From the outside, the King 95 3D Pro looks the part of its royal name. That signature curve and three panes of glass offer a panoramic view inside your case like few others, letting you show off your PC from even more angles. It also features a frosted, continuous LED strip running along the tiered top, right side, and bottom, adding some tasteful bling to the chassis. If you get the Pro version with the seven fans, it’s an RGB light show inside which could be polarizing. I do wish there were an option for preinstalled non-RGB fans, since the seven included ones and the infinity mirror styling may not be for everyone. Still, the curved front corner and clean lines really cement the King 95 3D as one of the better-looking panoramic cases on the market. Future Future Future Future Future Future Up front, the removable curved glass corner with a smoked tint sets it apart from most others. On the right, the front IO panel runs vertically, with the power button on top and the LED on/off button below. It has three USB ports: one 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C and two USB 3.2 Gen1 (5 Gbps) Type-A ports. Finally, it has a 3.5mm audio jack. That continuous 118-LED strip is visible from the front, running along the top, down the right edge, and along the bottom edge. I’m…

articles.title: AI100 report released: embodied AI highlighted as grand challenge
articles.content: The One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100) is a longitudinal study that assesses AI’s development and societal impact. Reports are released once every five years, with the 2026 edition the third in the series. The title of this year’s report is “AI Goes Mainstream: The Scaling Era and the Rise of Generative AI” . The panel behind the project is an international committee of experts tasked with examining AI’s evolution across technical, ethical, economic, and societal domains. They respond to 12 standing questions about AI’s advances, opportunities, dangers, and societal effects, and compare developments since 2021 with the previous panel’s assessments. The 2026 AI100 Study Panel report examines the scaling of data and computing resources behind generative AI, advances in scientific discovery, investment in AI infrastructure, the concentration of frontier AI development, cybersecurity and military applications, the trustworthiness of digital media, emerging risks, public participation, and international governance. One of the standing questions concerns open grand challenges in the field, with the experts highlighting six as particularly inspiring and scientifically important. Most relevant to the robotics community is the problem of physical AI and embodied intelligence . In the five years since the last AI100 report (published in 2021), we’ve witnessed integration of natural language processing (NLP) into robotic systems, the use of vision-language-action models for training and control, and advances in simulation technology which have allowed models trained in virtual settings to be deployed on physical hardware. The 2026 AI100 report notes that China is the leader in industrial robot development, deploying more robots than the rest of the world combined. China also produces about 80% of the world’s humanoid robots. Although this sector currently accounts for just 2% of the market, it is growing rapidly. Despite the progress of recent years, there remains a huge gap between the demonstration of capabilities and deployment. Many of the success stories have been in highly constrained environments (such as warehouses), or with very specific products (for example, floor cleaners). The key challenge remains the sheer complexity of the real world. Some of the scientific problems to overcome include long-horizon planning under uncertainty, achieving dexterous manipulation of diverse objects, and establishing formal performance guarantees. Whilst there are some practitioners who believe that the current statistical learning paradigms are sufficient for attacking these open problems, many others feel that fundamentally new ideas will be required to bring robot deployment into genuine real-world scenarios. It will be interesting to observe how this plays out over the next five years. You can read the report in full here .

articles.title: Nintendo unleashes DMCA takedown wave against open-source Switch modchip firmware, 144 tools disabled
articles.content: Nintendo has set its famously litigious sights on the open-source firmware that powers hardware modchips on Nintendo Switch. Earlier this week, GitHub posted a DCMA request from Nintendo of America confirming that an entire network of 144 total repositories, including the parent repository, was taken down. Mod chip firmware for hardware including SX Core, SX Lite, Picofly, and HWFLY was targeted. Early original Nintendo Switch consoles shipped with an unpatchable hardware exploit found in the device's recovery mode, which has since been patched in later units such as the Switch Lite and Switch OLED (the modchip hack doesn't work on Switch 2). As such, running custom software on patched Switches requires hardware modification, soldering a microchip like a Picofly, HWFLY, or SX Core to your Switch's motherboard. These chips require firmware, specifically code that can perform the voltage glitching required during boot to hack the Switch. Rather than playing whack-a-mole with vendors of off-the-shelf microcontrollers, Nintendo has instead issued a DCMA takedown notice to the entire family of GitHub repos hosting this firmware. "The reported repositories offer, link to, or otherwise provide access to mod chip firmware including but not limited to SX Core, SX Lite, Picofly, or HWFLY," the DCMA request from Nintendo reads. "The firmware allows Nintendo Switch modchips to illegally circumvent Nintendo’s TPMs in order to run illegal copies of Nintendo Switch games. Specifically, during operation, the mod chip firmware at the reported repositories circumvents the technological protection measures put in place on the Nintendo Switch console by bypassing the boot sequence. Nintendo went on to state that because these repositories are designed "primarily" to unlawfully circumvent technological measures controlling access to work protected under the DCMA, distributing mod chip firmware "constitutes unlawful trafficking in technology that is 'primarily designed or produced for the purpose of circumventing a technological measure that effectively controls access' to copyrighted works." In support of this argument, Nintendo cited criminal proceedings brought by the US Department of Justice against Team-Xecuter, a maker and seller of SX Pro, SX Core, and SX Lite modchips. While these modchips can be (and are) used for game piracy, they unlock a host of features including running homebrew and custom applications, emulation, alternative operating systems, and more. They also enable game modding, custom themes, and even Switch overclocking. Naturally, Nintendo has chosen to focus on their utility in accessing pirated games and bypassing DRM. Because much of this hardware and firmware is already out in the wild, the move won't have any impact on existing Switch owners who have a modchip installed. However, this will prevent firmware updates to existing modchips, as well as firmware flashing and reflashing. Naturally, it will also prevent future potential hardware modders from hacking their Switch in the same way. Nintendo is famous for its fervent prosecution of copyright law, but developments in AI are turning this into a drastically more complicated battle. Nintendo's Zelda remake was dumped online on the same day it launched on Switch 2 , while earlier this year one developer used AI to bring the original Nintendo 64 version to iOS. In July, Mario Kart Wii was recompiled for PC in 4K with over 200 tracks.

articles.title: Lava Security and OWASP Focus on the Overlooked Risks Behind GPU Cloud Infrastructure
articles.content: The security of an AI workload depends on more than the applications and models running on it. Beneath every deployment sits an extensive infrastructure environment responsible for processing, networking, storing, and managing the data required by artificial intelligence systems. As GPU cloud capacity becomes increasingly important to organizations running AI workloads, the security of that underlying environment deserves greater attention. Neocloud providers and AI data center operators must account for vulnerabilities involving hardware, firmware, networking technologies, management interfaces, and shared operational systems. Lava Security is bringing these issues into focus through its Top 10 Neocloud and AI Data Center Security Risks framework, which has become an official OWASP project . The initiative was developed by Yakir Kadkoda, CTO and Co-Founder of Lava Security, and Michael Katchinskiy, Head of Security Research. It is designed to help infrastructure providers, operators, and organizations purchasing GPU cloud capacity better understand the security challenges affecting AI environments. When Shared Infrastructure Creates New Exposure Modern AI data centers combine thousands of GPUs with high-speed networking, specialized management controllers, shared storage, and complex orchestration systems. Many of these technologies were originally designed for trusted high-performance computing environments. Their growing use in commercial neocloud environments, where unrelated organizations may share physical infrastructure, introduces additional security risks. Bare-metal neocloud deployments illustrate the issue. Customers may receive root access to rented servers, giving them substantial control over the computing environment. However, if management interfaces are not adequately restricted, that access could allow changes to hardware boot configurations. Those configurations may persist even after an operating system reinstall . If a server is subsequently reassigned without resetting the affected settings, another customer could inherit a compromised environment. This is one example of why infrastructure security requires visibility into components that conventional operating system and application protections may not cover. "AI infrastructure introduces attack surfaces that traditional security approaches may not adequately address. Organizations need to understand what happens below the operating system, particularly when hardware, firmware, and management interfaces are shared across customers," said Michael Katchinskiy, Head of Security Research at Lava Security. "This framework helps make those risks easier to identify and provides practical guidance for addressing them." A Wider Definition of AI Infrastructure Security The OWASP framework examines vulnerabilities across multiple layers of the infrastructure stack. Its coverage includes compromised server firmware, weaknesses in high-speed networking technologies such as InfiniBand and RDMA, inadequate tenant isolation, and insecure out-of-band management interfaces. It also considers supply chain threats, data center facility systems, shared storage and AI artifacts, incomplete security certifications, centralized operational services, and delays in vulnerability patching. These categories are intended to provide a broader picture of how infrastructure vulnerabilities can affect an entire environment. Each category includes potential attack scenarios, real-world implications, and practical mitigation recommendations. Infrastructure providers and operators can use this material to evaluate their environments and prioritize security improvements. For organizations purchasing GPU cloud capacity, the framework also offers a reference for understanding the controls protecting their workloads.
