articles.title: Cognichip reveals how its new AI-assisted program can slash chip design times from months to days — automating labor-intensive tasks cuts design time down, Chief Product Officer explains
articles.content: Amid the AI gold rush, one particularly fruitful vein of research is the emergence of AI-assisted workflows in electronic design automation ( EDA) tools like Cadence Maestro . One such company developing such foundational models is Cognichip, which in September launched Artificial Chip Intelligence (ACI), proprietary AI models developed specifically for semiconductor engineering. ACI deploys the 'industry’s largest training dataset' across semiconductor physics and chip design principles. ACI Enterprise is Cognichip's deployable platform, which combines these specialized models with agentic workflows, project memory, and computing infrastructure for AI inference. The company describes ACI's approach as a self-learning flywheel, a continuously evolving design environment that brings together specifications, register-transfer level (RTL), and verification results to build a design that meets power, performance, and area (PPA) targets to Pareto limits. We sat down with Cognichip to learn more. "We have surpassed, I think, over ten million training samples in our datasets that are either things that we designed ourselves directly or things that have been generated through our synthetic technology," says Stelios Diamantidis, Chief Product Officer at Cognichip, in an interview with Tom's Hardware Premium . "We have invented new ways of creating synthetic training samples for semiconductor design. And very importantly, now that we have all these data samples, characterized data samples, we also had to invent new models so that we can capture the data, and we also had to invent new pipelines for training so that we can map the training data to the models themselves." (Image credit: Cognichip) A self-learning flywheel Cognichip says ACI can analyze specifications, explore microarchitectural options, generate RTL, verify designs, identify and fix functional problems, and optimize designs to meet PPA targets. The system can also integrate existing IP modules and even produce FPGA implementations. In principle, ACI enables engineers to focus on product requirements and architectural decisions while ACI handles much of the logic implementation and verification work. "Build the spec, build the RTL, estimate PPA, perform optimizations, run verification, everything," Diamantidis told us while explaining how ACI can develop and evaluate multiple architectural alternatives before engineers select the preferred design. "We do not try to turn the designer into a verification engine; our system is self-verified, so we want the designer to design, and we want our system not only to do the tasks but also verify them." Because ACI operates as a self-learning flywheel, Cognichip claims engineers can revisit earlier architectural decisions and modify their designs without restarting the entire development process from scratch. "Architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, all abstractions in the cognitive system are aligned, so the change in microarchitecture is essentially automatically reflected in RTL, and vice versa," Diamantidis explained. "Changes in RTL are automatically reflected in microarchitecture." Cognichip says it has participated in more than 40 customer engagements, including projects at Renesas and SiTime. According to the company, these engagements span a wide range of chip designs, from microcontrollers and encryption engines to networking processors, RISC-V CPUs, and AI accelerators. To illustrate ACI's capabilities, Cognichip points to an evaluation conducted with an unnamed leading fabless semiconductor company. The customer provided an existing 55-page microarchitecture specification, which ACI used to explore architecture options, develop RTL from scratch, and integrate middleware and other components. The system also generated SystemVerilog testbenches, ran simulations, identified and corrected errors, and achieved functional verification closure with over 90% UVM coverage, the company claims. articles.title: 2013 breach at Russian cybercrime forum resurfaces with millions of victims' credentials
articles.content: A 2013 breach of Russian-language cybercrime forum YouHack exposed its members' login details – and millions of credentials they had posted about other victims, according to newly cataloged data. Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) added the breach on Wednesday, recording 7.2 million unique email addresses. Around 107,000 belonged to forum members, whose exposed data included usernames, IP addresses, and mostly unsalted MD5 password hashes. Unsalted MD5 is a poor choice for protecting passwords. It's fast to compute, allowing attackers to test guesses at speed, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Hardly good hygiene for a hacking forum. You might expect members of a cybercrime forum to know better than to reuse passwords or register with an email address tied to their real identity. Expectations and reality are not always on speaking terms, as AlphaBay founder Alexandre Cazes demonstrated. YouHack, a longtime cybercrime forum, moved to a different domain after the 2013 breach and remains active, giving cybercrims a place to trade stolen credentials and financial data. The data collated from that digital burglary was eventually bundled into 2024's so-called Mother of all Breaches – a 12TB, 26 billion-record mega-dump of files taken from myriad data security lapses. Millions more HIBP separately published its findings concerning another Russian data breach today. It said the 2023 breach of Russian bank Sberbank's loyalty program (SberSpasibo) contained records belonging to 48 million users. The dataset included 3.3 million unique email addresses, alongside phone numbers and dates of birth. Bank card numbers were stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, which could let attackers test possible numbers against the leaked hashes for a match. Reporting on the SberSpasibo breach at the time suggested the records were dated between April 2017 and February 2022, and the attack was claimed by the pro-Ukraine hacktivist outfit NLB. NLB also claimed responsibility for an attack on Sberbank's internal systems at the same time, and later took partial credit for an attack on Alfa-Bank , Russia's largest private bank. ®

articles.title: Manny Pacquiao’s MannyPay Wants to Lower Credit Card Fees for U.S. Small Businesses
articles.content: Manny Pacquiao's name now appears on a business most customers will never notice when they shop. MannyPay Global , which launched its U.S. merchant-processing division in July, is concerned with the machinery behind a card payment and how much a merchant pays to accept it. The eight-division boxing world champion is the company's founder and chairman. His involvement brings a recognizable name to a crowded financial-services market, though the businesses MannyPay hopes to reach are considerably less famous. Independent restaurants, neighborhood retailers and family-owned shops are among the merchants the company wants to serve. For these businesses, accepting a payment is rarely as simple as the customer tapping a card. There are processing charges to account for, equipment to maintain and sometimes several different services involved in keeping sales running. MannyPay's U.S. launch is built around the idea that merchants could benefit from handling more of that work through one provider. Pacquiao has connected the venture to the same interest in economic opportunity that has informed his philanthropic work and public service in the Philippines. "Throughout my life I have believed in creating opportunities that help people succeed," he said in the company's launch announcement. "MannyPay was built with that same purpose." MannyPay is targeting Filipino-owned businesses first MannyPay is starting with Filipino-owned businesses in the U.S., where the Pacquiao name already means something. Those businesses run from restaurants to grocery stores, and the cost math changes with each one. A restaurant needs a point-of-sale system that can handle a packed Saturday night. A grocery store needs checkout to keep moving on small, frequent purchases. For a family business, a jump in monthly processing costs comes out of the same money that pays for inventory or the next hire. The U.S. offer covers in-store terminals, online payments, recurring billing and electronic bank payments. MannyPay also takes on merchants in industries where underwriting is tougher In August, it added a second processing option through iMerchant, an international payments company, powered by Adyen. That one is for merchants with more complicated needs, like businesses selling across borders. Jas Mathur, Jimmy Virk and Martin Khemmoro lead MannyPay Chief executive Jas Mathur has spent more than 25 years building businesses across several industries, including financial services and e-commerce. His background includes working with merchants, whose concerns are often quite different from those of the banks and financial institutions that support payment processing. President Jimmy Virk brings more than 15 years in payments and is also the founder and CEO of Beyond Bancard. Martin Khemmoro , an executive vice president at MannyPay, contributes experience in international banking relationships and cross-border commerce through his leadership at iMerchant. Their responsibilities become particularly relevant as the company expands beyond straightforward card acceptance. A merchant that sells both online and in person may need compatible systems, and a business taking orders internationally can encounter payment methods and banking requirements unfamiliar to a local retailer. MannyPay says more financial services are coming as the U.S. business grows, and its website already previews a digital wallet and remittance product. Neither is available yet. What merchants can sign up for today is processing. Merchants have no shortage of processors to pick from. The ones who switch to MannyPay will do it for the rate in the contract, and for a person who picks up the phone when the terminal goes down in the middle of the dinner rush.

articles.title: Unpatched exploit allows malicious iOS apps to steal data
articles.content: Crypto exchange Binance is warning iPhone users of a security vulnerability in iOS that could allow a malicious app to steal data from other apps on the device. The exploit can allow malicious apps to get data used by others Finance apps have a big interest in maintaining security, especially when it comes to their own apps. Sometimes that protectiveness results in a warning that affects the operating system itself. In a post to X on November 10 , crypto app Binance warns of a vulnerability that affects multiple versions of iOS , including iOS 26.7.1 , 27.0.1, and iOS 27.2 This time, it's not a problem specific to Binance's app, but instead it is referred to as an "iOS-level issue," affecting practically all apps, reports Yahoo Finance . articles.title: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you. To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud. Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be . —Antonio Regalado This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands. MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks? Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify. The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models. Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology. The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. articles.title: iPhone Duo photography overview: Great cameras that suffer in extreme low light
articles.content: If you're holding off on an iPhone Duo solely because of camera concerns, you probably don't need to, but you will miss the advantages offered by pro iPhones. iPhone Duo has a capable camera system I've spent the past few weeks thinking hard about my place as a photographer and my iPhone's position in it. There is no doubt that Apple's iPhone has been a camera powerhouse for over a decade, but I'm increasingly aware of how few "pro" features I actually need. I never needed to confront this reality directly since Apple's most desirable iPhone was also the most "pro." I could grab whatever iPhone Pro Max and be happy knowing I'd have every photography feature available without compromise. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Exclusive: Nubank Alum Raises $14M For Colombia’s Palomma To Tackle Rent Payments, Landlord Financing
articles.content: In 2020, Cipriano Echavarría was working at Morgan Stanley in New York and weighing his next career move when he noticed a plaque on his desk. Among the names of people who had sat there before him was David Vélez . He looked up the name. Vélez was not only a fellow Colombian from his hometown of Medellín, but also the founder of Brazilian digital bank Nubank . Echavarría took a photo of the plaque and messaged him on LinkedIn , asking for career advice. It turned out that Vélez had an opportunity for Echavarria: Nubank was about to announce its expansion into Colombia and hire a launch team. By late 2020, Echavarría had returned home to join it, with plans to eventually start a company of his own. Felipe Monsalve, Cipriano Echavarría and Nicolás Gómez del Campo, founders of Palomma. (Courtesy photo) Now Echavarría’s Medellín-based startup, Palomma , has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Mexican venture firm Cometa to expand its financial services business for landlords, tenants and property managers, Crunchbase News has exclusively learned. The financing brings Palomma’s total funding to $14 million, including $4 million in previously undisclosed funding, according to Echavarría, its co-founder and CEO. Participants include Volpe Capital , Clocktower Technology Ventures , Tekton Ventures , Simma Capital and Yango Ventures , alongside existing investors Y Combinator , 17Sigma , Nido Ventures and Norte Ventures . Palomma says its annual recurring revenue has grown thirtyfold in 18 months to about $3 million. It processes about $130 million in monthly rental payments, serving more than 200,000 tenants through over 500 property managers in Colombia. It estimates $1.5 billion in annualized rent payment volume. The company will use the funding to expand in Colombia, develop additional AI and financial products, and prepare to enter other markets. It is considering Mexico, Brazil and the Spanish-speaking U.S. market, although Echavarría said Colombia remains the priority. “We want to win Colombia,” he said in an interview. Finding a business in rent payments Palomma’s business combines software that helps property managers handle leasing inquiries, customer service and collections with a payments system for collecting rent and paying landlords. Those relationships let it sell financing, rental guarantees, and other financial products to tenants and property owners. After nearly two years at Nubank, Echavarría went on to found Palomma with Felipe Monsalve and Nicolás Gómez del Campo , MIT -trained engineers with experience at Meta , Cobre and JP Morgan . The founders entered Y Combinator in January 2023 intending to build an account-to-account payments processor for Spanish-speaking Latin America. Growth was largely flat during the first year, Echavarría said. But then property managers began asking for help collecting rent. It soon became apparent that there were problems on both sides of the transaction. Tenants paid rent early in the month, but got their paychecks in twice-monthly installments. Meanwhile, landlords depended on rental income but struggled to borrow against it or protect themselves when tenants stopped paying. Property managers handled collections and payouts through labor-intensive processes, Echavarría said. Rather than acquire tenants and landlords as customers individually, Palomma decided to reach them through the companies managing their properties. The team decided, “let’s basically use the property managers as a distribution channel,” Echavarría recalled. From software to financial services Property managers get access to Palomma’s AI software, which handles tasks such as leasing conversations. It then offers to process their rent payments. Those payments give the company a record of rental income and tenant payment histories that it can use to assess applicants for financial products. From there, Palomma offers services for both tenants and landlords. Palomma Plus gives tenants rewards and…

articles.title: Democrats are back. So is economist Stephanie Kelton’s big idea
articles.content: In the early days of the Biden administration, after the COVID-19 pandemic and overlapping recession , advocates of government spending to aid the recovery faced concerns that such programs would add to the seemingly ever-growing national debt. In addition to arguments about unemployment and the overall health of the economy, backers of spending bills like what became the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act had an increasingly influential economic idea on their side. Modern Monetary Theory , or MMT, arose from the work of numerous economists, but it was especially popularized by the work of Stephanie Kelton , an economics professor who was a senior economic advisor to Senator Bernie Sanders’s presidential campaigns in 2016 and 2020 and served as chief economist for the Democratic staff of the Senate Budget Committee toward the end of the Obama administration. MMT, in essence, argues that deficit spending by governments with the power to issue their own currency isn’t inherently bad. And, as Kelton argued in her influential 2020 book The Deficit Myth , it can be used to promote a more prosperous and just economy. Common analogies between government deficit spending and consumers racking up credit card bills to spend beyond their means miss the mark, MMT’s advocates argue. “The work that I do explains why the federal government’s budget doesn’t work like a household budget, and why there is more capacity to spend on priorities, whether it’s healthcare, education, infrastructure, climate,” says Kelton. “Whatever it is, the spending capacity is there.” Since 2020, we’ve seen the end of the pandemic, the rise of inflation, and the reelection of Donald Trump, who despite pledges to shrink the size of government and limit international involvement has spent heavily on immigration enforcement and the war with Iran . Now, with a historic wave of Democrats set to take office in the House, Senate, and state governments across the country after campaigning on promises of affordability, MMT may again be poised to influence the direction of government. “I know that the book has been read, and the ideas have reached many of the candidates who are now getting prepared to take office in the Senate and House and across the country,” says Kelton, who today serves as a professor of economics and public policy at Stony Brook University, where she’s been based since 2017. ‘Spending always has consequences’ One of the earliest academic proponents of what became known as MMT is L. Randall Wray, today a professor of economics at the Levy Economics Institute of Bard College. Kelton studied under Wray at the University of Denver early in her career, and the two were later both based at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, where they were affiliated with the Center for Full Employment and Price Stability. At first, their research on monetary theory struggled to gain acceptance in the academic world, Wray says. “We had funding, so we could have conferences, and we wrote academic papers,” Wray says. “We gave presentations at academic conferences, and I can tell you none of that had an impact. We were trying to change the economic discipline, and it did not want to be changed.” What did help make a difference was a blog, New Economic Perspectives , founded by Kelton in time for both the 2000s blogosphere boom and the questioning of established economic wisdom in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis and Great Recession. “I sort of thought it was a waste of time—this was very early in the blogosphere,” Wray recalls. “But the blog took off, and really, that’s how MMT got to be known.” New Economic Perspectives drew the attention of readers in both the formal economics world and beyond, sparking online debates with other prominent economists, including the Nobel laureate and longtime New York Times columnist Paul Krugman. “By the time Krugman heard about it, I don’t know the number, but I would say there…

articles.title: Apple tells its Support Community to STFU
articles.content: Apple has abruptly stopped accepting new posts on its Support Community, putting the forum into read-only mode ahead of permanent closure on November 20, 2026. Users seeking help with their gizmos from other Apple customers were greeted with the message : "The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. "We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products." Need help? Head to the official Apple Support site. Want to see if your fellow Apple users have an answer to what ails your device? This is no longer the forum for you. Some reports date the site's origins to 1998, when Apple was busy killing off the Newton platform and launching Mac OS 8.5. Technology has come a long way since then, and recent AI developments have made user-to-user forums like Apple's Support Community less popular. Other places to seek advice remain, and useful answers were never guaranteed. As one user put it on X : "rip to every thread that ended with 'same problem here' and zero solutions." Still, it's an abrupt end to almost three decades of accumulated advice, troubleshooting, and unanswered questions. Apple hasn't said whether that archive will remain accessible after the closure. The Register asked Apple for the reasoning behind the termination. The company has yet to respond. ®
articles.author: Richard Speed

articles.title: Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft
articles.content: Shipping behemoth A.P. Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured. "Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said . "The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI." Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations. Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available. "Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact. "As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact. "Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident." Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017. Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy. Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU). Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill , owing to remediation and rebuild costs. Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days. In 2020, as exclusively revealed by The Register , Maersk went on to lay off around 150 staffers from its command and control center in Maidenhead, England. The staffers who lost their jobs had played key roles in the recovery. ®
articles.author: Connor Jones

articles.title: How Portland is spending its tax on billion-dollar companies
articles.content: On a former landfill in Portland, Oregon, workers are installing hundreds of solar panels in a community solar project that will help people living nearby save on their electric bills. The new solar farm was funded by an unusual source: the city’s pioneering tax on billion-dollar corporations, which was enacted in November 2018 and has raised more than $1.7 billion to fund hundreds of climate-related projects. The first-of-its-kind program, created through a citizen-led ballot measure, charges a 1% tax on the local retail sales of large corporations like Amazon and Walmart. The city hasn’t disclosed which companies have to pay, but it applies to corporations with more than $1 billion in annual retail sales and at least $500,000 in sales within Portland city limits, with some exemptions for necessities like groceries. Around 500 large companies are affected, and the revenue goes both to community grants and larger city projects, with a focus on climate justice. Turning a landfill into a community asset In the case of the solar farm, around 170 low-income families can sign up to use a portion of the electricity that’s generated. Because the city fund is covering the cost of putting in the solar panels, the project immediately creates steep savings for those customers—as much as 40% less than what people were paying on their utility bills before. “Without those funds, it wouldn’t exist,” says Jessica Carmona, the renewables program director at the Bonneville Environmental Foundation , a nonprofit working on the project. “It’s not possible to build these types of sites for nonprofits that are low-income benefiting, with such high levels of savings, if you’re not getting funding.” [Photo: The Bird Alliance of Oregon] The solar farm sits on land now owned by the nonprofit Bird Alliance of Oregon , which is using another grant from the city fund to restore wildlife habitat on the former landfill. A high school across the street has gotten grants for youth climate action. On the same street, the city has used grant money to plant trees to help reduce extreme heat, and another grant will help fund a major new rapid bus corridor. From a ‘bike bus’ to clean energy retrofits Changes are rolling out throughout Portland, thanks to grants from the Portland Clean Energy Community Benefits Fund, which administers the revenue from the 1% tax. The latest round of grants includes expanding a “ bike bus” program to help kids get to school safely on bikes—with the goal to ultimately help replace more than half a million miles in car trips to school—and another program that lets employees at a local university borrow bikes for their commute to work. Other grants support access to EVs . Another Bird Alliance grant is expanding a program that works with homeowners to restore habitat in their backyards , creating a network that connects to parks; while it helps wildlife, it’s also adding shade and helping clean the air for people. “What [the Portland Clean Energy Fund] is allowing us to do is to work with a total of 420 new households focused in areas that have the greatest burdens of urban heat islands and air pollution and low tree canopy,” says Micah Meskel, the director of conservation and rehabilitation at the Bird Alliance of Oregon. At its core, Meskel says, the city fund is a climate justice program. He argues that it’s fitting that corporations “who have the most negative impact on climate change be the ones that are paying for it.” The Bird Alliance, along with other nonprofits in the city, helped fight for the original ballot measure after seeing a need for more funding to tackle the growing impacts of climate change. Grant money is also helping retrofit homes to reduce energy bills, and training workers to perform energy audits. The grants have helped the city respond to climate impacts that are happening faster than expected—after a deadly heat wave in 2021 , for example, grants helped residents get air conditioners so…

articles.title: Apple Chip Supplier TSMC Approves $1 Billion AI Investment
articles.content: Apple chip supplier TSMC has announced board approval to invest up to $1 billion in AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic. The decision allows TSMC to buy up to $500 million of shares in each company. The board also authorized up to $500 million to create a company that will invest in semiconductor businesses and the wider industry. TSMC manufactures Apple's custom chips, while OpenAI and Anthropic are developing processors of their own. The investments deepen TSMC's ties with companies that compete with Apple for its most advanced manufacturing capacity, as well as in the AI space more broadly. OpenAI is rumored to be working on hardware to rival Apple directly. articles.title: The smartphone isn’t dead. But the battle to replace it is already on
articles.content: The smartphone changed the world, but listening to some tech bosses lately, you’d be forgiven for thinking AI could threaten its dominance. The emerging debate about what comes after the smartphone is about much more than device sales. It’s about who controls the gateway to the customer, and who gets a cut of the money they spend. And that battle has already begun. Amazon has blocked Meta’s AI assistant, Muse, from shopping on its e-commerce platform. The tech giants are already fighting over who gets between businesses and their customers. Tellingly, Sam Altman, the OpenAI boss, has questioned the smartphone’s future. He argues that these gadgets are ill-suited to artificial intelligence. I don’t think the smartphone is about to fall off a cliff. Apple’s iPhone pulled in $54.3 billion in sales in the three months to June 2026, a 22% rise on the year before. Unit shipments also shot up 15%, the tech analysis company IDC estimates. If the smartphone loses its dominance at all, it’ll be a slow burn, unlike its rapid rise, having overtaken PC shipments just three and a half years after the iPhone launched in 2007. However, the smartphone’s stranglehold on how we access the digital world could be challenged by new technologies. Smart glasses are jostling for pole position. But they come with drawbacks, including added weight and limited battery life. One independent tester burned through half the battery in Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses in just an hour of heavy video use. And let’s face it: They look pretty dorky too. For all the hype, they’re still David to the smartphone’s Goliath. Analysts forecast 15 million pairs will have shipped this year, a drop in the ocean compared to more than a billion smartphones. So it’ll probably take a combination of technologies to knock the smartphone off its perch. One is Apple’s AirPods wireless earphones. They already provide hands-free access to Siri, its voice assistant. But a recent AI upgrade now allows some users to hold chatbot-style conversations with them. Apple is also reportedly developing AirPods with built-in cameras, to give Siri eyes as well as ears. You could look at ingredients and ask for a recipe, say, or get walking directions based on your surroundings, without pulling out your smartphone. Facebook’s parent Meta, meanwhile, plans to launch the stand-alone device Muse Charm. It’s small enough to hang from a keychain; a screen and voice controls provide access to Muse, Meta’s AI assistant. Muse itself has exploded in popularity since its September launch, quickly becoming the most downloaded app in the U.S. The battle for control The battle to control the next digital interface is likely to be fought on three fronts: hardware, distribution, and intelligence. Apple is a heavyweight in hardware, owing to its $146 billion cash and investment pile, engineering prowess and 2.5 billion active devices. Huawei and Samsung are also contenders. In the distribution layer, Amazon has upgraded Alexa with AI, enabling users to have natural conversations with the voice assistant, and for it to carry out tasks such as booking restaurants. Alexa is already connected to more than 600 million devices. Google’s AI-powered search summaries reach more than 2.5 billion people monthly. And Google’s Android software powers more than 3 billion devices worldwide. Meta is another contender. Beyond selling hardware, it could become a powerful middleman, taking a cut of transactions handled by its AI assistant, from shopping to travel bookings. Amazon has likewise considered taking a cut of purchases handled by Alexa, even as it blocks Muse from shopping on its platform. The third battleground is intelligence, where the frontier AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic are frontrunners. OpenAI is also muscling into hardware; it acquired Io, Sir Jony Ive’s startup, for $6.5 billion. The former Apple design chief and OpenAI are developing AI-powered devices, which could give ChatGPT a direct route to consumers…
articles.author: Amit Joshi

articles.title: The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry
articles.content: This article is brought to you by Innomotics . In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics , a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants. 1866: The breakthrough that powered the future The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century. This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. Innomotics The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today. One principle. Millions of motors. More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems. Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations. Innomotics Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades. Award-winning innovations Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award. Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements. Innomotics AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime,…

articles.title: The bad news for Microsoft in the Blue Tsunami
articles.content: Elections have consequences — and big elections have big consequences. Few have been bigger than last week’s US midterms, featuring a Blue Tsunami that swept aside Republican control of Congress and signaled the end of Trumpism. Those consequences will especially be felt by Big Tech and Big AI. Voters made it clear that they don’t want data centers in their backyards. They voted for candidates who vowed to rein in AI, and those who promised to investigate the cozy relationship between tech companies and President Trump. And they voted for candidates who promised to put an end to rampant government corruption tied to tech billionaires. Microsoft didn’t go all-in on Trump as so many Big Tech firms did. The company held fast to core values like diversity, equity, and inclusion in its hiring and employment practices. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t attend Trump’s inauguration as other tech CEOs including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Google’s Sundar Pichai, and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk did. He didn’t fawn over Trump like Apple’s Tim Cook , who gave Trump a 24-carat gold plaque and attended the gala White House screening of the Amazon-funded Melania documentary held on the day US Immigration and Custom Enforcement (ICE) agents murdered Alex Pretti in Minnesota. Microsoft even fired its law firm because the firm agreed to provide Trump with $125 million in pro bono work, replacing it with a firm that sued Trump. But in other ways, Microsoft has played nice with the Trump administration, including donating millions of dollars for his White House ballroom project. So Microsoft is no more protected than other tech companies against what comes next under the Democratic Congress. In this column I’ll look at the potential bad news for the company. In the next I’ll look at how Microsoft might benefit from the election. Investigate, investigate, investigate The voting was barely over when top Democratics made clear that one of their first orders of business would be investigations and public hearings into Big Tech and Big AI. Microsoft will be among the companies investigated. Two days after election day, Senator Richard Blumenthal demanded that the FCC and tech companies including Microsoft, Apple, Meta, Google, Nvidia, Amazon and others turn over documents related to the companies’ donations to Trump for his new ballroom. That’s part of an investigation that will look into conflicts of interest and quid pro quos. The Washington Post reported that Microsoft donated $10 million to the project. If the companies didn’t turn over the documents, Blumenthal warned, they’d face subpoenas when he becomes chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations when the new Congress convenes in January. That’s only the first investigation of many to come. Senator Ed Markey, who has locked horns with Microsoft and other tech firms in the past, posted on X on election night: “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.” No free ride for data centers One of the midterm election’s biggest issues was the data centers Microsoft and other AI giants have been building. Critics say the centers increase electricity costs, and that residents are subsidizing tech companies by bearing those higher costs. “Data centers raised wholesale [electricity] prices by 6.9 percent nationally by 2025,” the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas reported . Critics also complain of data centers’ water use, noise level, pollution, and taking away both open space and local control from communities. Forty out of 41 local ballot initiatives against the centers won. Democratic governors, senators, and state officials promised crackdowns. Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a think tank, told the New York Times , “Expect a tsunami of new rules and oversight.” That’s bad news for Microsoft. The company has already said that it can’t build data centers fast enough to meet demand for its AI services.…

articles.content: Ancient Slashdot reader Lank writes: GTA VI is now available for preloading. The download weighs in at a whopping 210+ gigabytes on the PS5! Start downloading now and remember to take Nov. 19th off from work. "On Xbox, preloads for digital versions went live at 12 a.m. GMT on November 10 for Series X and Series S, which translates to 7 p.m. EST / 6 p.m. CST / 5 p.m. MST / 4 p.m. PT on Monday, November 9," notes PCMag. "For PlayStation 5 and PS5 Pro owners, preloading started on Tuesday, November 10 at midnight local time." "If you ordered a physical copy of GTA 6, games will begin arriving at retailers and shipping to buyers on November 12. You can use the code in your box to preload your copy of the game." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Adobe opens Creative Cloud apps to third-party AI assistants
articles.content: Adobe will open its Creative Cloud applications to third-party AI assistants, with the ability to edit content in Photoshop, After Effects, Illustrator, and Premiere from tools such as ChatGPT or Claude, the company announced at its Max event. The model context protocol (MCP) integration, due in private beta in early 2027, would let third-party AI assistants to make changes to content in Creative Cloud desktop applications, without losing the ability to adjust individual elements of a design or video manually afterwards. For example, a third-party AI assistant could remove a logo from multiple advertising campaign assets. “Make the change once, then ask your agent to cascade it across the rest of the campaign, and step in at any moment to refine the work by hand,” said Deepa Subramaniam, Adobe’s VP, product marketing for Creative Cloud, in a blog post Tuesday. Third-party agents could also connect to other apps in a single workflow, so it would be possible to “pull in a project brief from Google Docs, work on it in Adobe’s tools and share the result with your team via Slack,” for example, Subramaniam said. The MCP connections can help creative professionals “keep their work where they choose to work, without sacrificing the upside of modern collaborative and secure systems,” said Liz Miller, vice president and principal analyst at Constellation Research. “End users … have always relied on multiple tools to capture their taste and bring it to life. For them, these connections are another tool that opens up access to so much more of their toolkit.” Keith Kirkpatrick, vice president of research at The Futurum Group, also anticipates demand from Adobe users to access Creative Cloud apps via third-party AI assistants, though he expects it will appeal most to a “fairly specific crowd” of “creative technologists, production teams, and power users who already spend their day in Claude or ChatGPT and want an agent to take care of the tedious stuff: organizing assets, setting up layers, building out sequences.” “Most creative pros are still going to want their hands in the application,” he said. Opening access to Creative Cloud apps via third-party agents could potentially loosen the direct relationship Adobe has with customers — a scenario that many software vendors are now grappling with. For Adobe, it’s a necessary adaptation, as employees increase their use of AI assistants to get work done. “Companies are using several AI models at once, and people are starting more of their work inside these assistants,” said Kirkpatrick. “If that’s where the request starts, Adobe wants to be the one doing the work behind it.” Gartner predicts that enterprise AI assistants will account for more of knowledge workers’ daily interaction time than any other application within the next three years, according to a recent Magic Quadrant report . Miller said that opening its applications to third-party tools could be beneficial for Adobe’s business. “This won’t negatively impact Adobe’s place with their core creative, marketing, or business users,” she said. “In fact, the flexibility will give their customers options in where and how to get work done. “For users who have found their flow and patterns of work in ChatGPT or Claude, [they can] stay there but still access the skills and tools you need to use to generate the quality of work expected,” Miller said. The MCP integration in Creative Cloud is the latest part of Adobe’s strategy to embrace third-party AI assistants — Adobe has previously announced ChatGPT, Claude, and Google Gemini integrations that provide limited editing capabilities for apps such as Acrobat, Photoshop, Premiere, Express, and Lightroom, directly within the AI assistants. This contrasts with the new MCP integrations that let AI assistants make changes directly to content in Adobe’s desktop applications. “The real question is whether any of this turns into paying Adobe customers, and Adobe hasn’t shown that yet with its existing…

articles.title: Your new Android speed-typing superpower
articles.content: When we talk about more efficient text entry on Android, we’re typically talkin’ about one of two things: Tips for tapping into little-known shortcuts and extras within your existing on-screen keyboard Smarter voice input systems for faster and easier speech-to-text transcription Those areas of improvement are all well and good — and plenty important, without a doubt! — but when it comes to serious productivity and work communication, there’s one more type of tool that can make a monumental difference and yet virtually never comes up in the Android typing conversation. It’s the type of tool that lots of smart workers already embrace on the desktop front but that’s far less common in the mobile world, where it’s if anything even more useful — and that’s an intelligent text expander. Text expanders let you create and save common phrases or even entire paragraphs of text you find yourself typing often and then insert ’em into any text field, anywhere, with a quick ‘n’ simple keyboard command. There’s one such tool on Android that stands out above the rest, and it just got a massive makeover that makes it even more of an indispensable addition. Lemme show ya how it works and what it’s all about. [Psst: Want even more advanced Android knowledge? Check out my free Android Shortcut Supercourse to learn tons of time-saving tricks for your phone.] Your Android text expander advantage My fellow Android-appreciating animal, allow me to introduce — or maybe re -introduce — you to a handy little tool called Typing Hero . Typing Hero first popped up on my radar a few years ago . But it’s come a really long way since, especially with its recent revamp, and it’s well worth bringing to the surface now as a potential new piece of your Android productivity toolbox. On the simplest possible level, what Typing Hero does is allow you to create prewritten text snippets and then map ’em to specific keyboard commands — short and memorable abbreviations like *thx or *omw that you can type into any text field, using whatever regular Android keyboard app you already use, and then have your full snippet appear right in that same place. It’s so easy and so effective, it genuinely gives me a jolt of joy every time I see it happen: Typing Hero in action, with its most basic text expanding feature. JR Raphael, Foundry Setting up snippets is super-simple, too: You just go into the Typing Hero app, create a new snippet, and put in whatever keyword and result you want. Creating new snippets in Typing Hero is surprisingly simple. JR Raphael, Foundry That in and of itself is such a smart time-saver, especially if you tend to type the same sorts of stock responses over and over while you’re dealing with emails, Slack messages, or any other kind of communication. And honestly, that’s what’ll make Typing Hero worth having in place for most of us. But the app gets even more interesting when you start to explore some of its extra-advanced options — for instance, being able to map multiple snippets to a single trigger keyword and then get a pop-up menu to choose from anytime you enter the term. Triggering multiple related snippets is a powerful Typing Hero possibility. JR Raphael, Foundry Typing Hero also supports all sorts of advanced commands for actual actions on Android — like automatically hitting send and then moving back to the previous screen as a part of a single keyword. Text expansion alongside actual system-level actions makes for a pretty incredible pairing. JR Raphael, Foundry Not bad for step-saving, right? Beyond that, Typing Hero can incorporate a bunch of different variables into its snippets — so, for instance, you might have it automatically insert whatever text was most recently copied into your Android system clipboard as a part of a snippet or automatically insert the current date or time. You can even configure it to pause for your input and ask you to fill in certain blank variables whenever a snippet is activated — if, say, you want to…

articles.title: This former Facebook employee wants to show AI in all its glory—and all its flaws
articles.content: Americans, in case you hadn’t heard, are growing weary of AI . Just one in nine Americans supports AI data center construction in their community, according to a poll from the University of Massachusetts Amherst . A Pew Research Center survey found that 67% have little or no confidence in the federal government’s ability to regulate artificial intelligence effectively. And perhaps most tellingly, 54% of Americans say they’re simply tired of hearing about AI, according to a Talker Research survey . Amid the nonstop barrage of headlines about AI’s risks and hype, it’s easy to lose sight of what the tech is actually accomplishing. Dave Goldblatt, a product engineer at Mission Control AI and former Facebook employee, wants to change that. He’s the creator of Because of AI , an independent, unfunded research database that tracks documented cases in which AI has delivered measurable benefits in fields ranging from medicine and education to transportation and accessibility. Rather than tout the tech’s theoretical potential, the site focuses on real-world outcomes, evaluating each case based on the strength of its evidence, how directly the results can be attributed to AI, and when the impact occurred. Crucially, the database also documents cases where AI has not delivered on its promise. ‘It can be a great thing, or it could be a terrible thing’ Goldblatt’s inspiration came from a subscriber chat for The Exponential View , a newsletter by the British tech entrepreneur Azeem Azhar . When another chat member asked whether anyone had compiled a dashboard of measurable improvements to human life attributable to AI, Goldblatt turned to Claude to assemble a list. The response was enthusiastic enough that he decided to build an entire website around the idea. (It took him just four hours.) Since launching on October 23, Because of AI has operated largely autonomously; AI tools continually update its database. The site is attracting between 200 and 300 visitors a day, according to Goldblatt. “It’s automated now, so I’m just gonna have my machines continue to update, continue to monitor, and slowly build up the audience,” Goldblatt tells Fast Company . The site organizes its findings into three categories: “Because of AI,” “Not Because,” and “Not Yet.” Among its documented successes is an AI-assisted tuberculosis screening program in Ethiopia, which identified 1,660 cases between January 2025 and March 2026 in settings where no radiologists were available to interpret X-rays. Not every deployment has been so successful. An AI-enabled stethoscope introduced at 205 National Health Service general practices in the U.K., for instance, failed to significantly improve heart failure detection after 12 months. But the database also makes a point to say that a disappointing outcome doesn’t necessarily mean the AI is ineffective. Poor implementation, inadequate training, or difficulties integrating AI into existing workflows can all undermine its effectiveness. “Everyone who is involved in tech and works in AI knows that it is tremendously powerful, and, of course, like anything that’s tremendously powerful, it can be a great thing, or it could be a terrible thing,” Goldblatt says. “At the very least, we can establish some sort of a ground truth inasmuch as ground truth exists anymore.” A second project Goldblatt is applying a similar approach to another project, albeit one with a more pointed focus. His second website, Pundit Claims , scrutinizes public statements by the prominent AI critics Gary Marcus and Ed Zitron, evaluating whether the available evidence supports their assertions. Goldblatt establishes the criteria for evaluating claims, while AI models handle the drafting and fact-checking. Models from Anthropic and OpenAI review the findings before a verdict is published. articles.title: Make Apple Watch Listen for Sounds Like the Doorbell
articles.content: One of Apple's accessibility features on iPhone can listen for important sounds around you, such as a doorbell, siren or alarm, and it sends you a notification when it hears one. The feature has been extended to Apple's new Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 models, so the alert reaches your wrist even when your iPhone isn't with you. It's especially useful for people who are deaf or hard of hearing, but it has everyday uses too. If you wear noise-cancelling headphones while working and don't want to miss the doorbell – if you're expecting a delivery, for example – your Apple Watch can alert you. Sounds Your Apple Watch Can Detect Sound Recognition can detect the following 15 sounds. Any you switch on in the iPhone's Sounds list are also detected by your Apple Watch when "Detect using Apple Watch" is enabled: Fire Alarm Siren Smoke Alarm Cat Dog Appliances Car Horn Doorbell Door Knock Glass Breaking Kettle Water Running Baby Crying Coughing Shouting If a sound isn't recognized automatically, you can also teach your iPhone a Custom Alarm or Custom Appliance or Doorbell from the same Sounds list. What You'll Need You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4 paired with an iPhone 11 or later, or an iPhone SE (2nd generation or later), running iOS 27. If you already use Sound Recognition on your iPhone, it turns on automatically for your Apple Watch, so you may not need to do anything. Either way, here's how to set it up: Open the Settings app on your iPhone and tap Accessibility . In the "Hearing" section, tap Sound & Name Recognition . Tap Sound Recognition and turn on the Sound Recognition toggle, then turn on Detect using Apple Watch . Tap Sounds and turn on the sounds you want to hear about, such as Doorbell . You can also choose a specific alert tone for each sound. Apple says Sound Recognition is processed on your Apple Watch and iPhone and doesn't record or store audio. It shouldn't be treated as a safety system, though. You shouldn't rely on it in situations where you may be harmed or injured, in high-risk or emergency situations, or for navigation, per Apple's guidelines. articles.title: ‘They don’t understand hackers’: Cybersecurity pros explain why everyone panicking about AI-powered hacks is wrong
articles.content: As head of counter-adversary operations at CrowdStrike , Adam Meyers has a front-row seat to the threats facing companies. Yet even for him, a recent trip to South Korea was out of the ordinary. As he was preparing to sleep on the flight from the United States, Meyers received a message from colleagues informing him that six Korean banks had been hacked and that he would likely face questions about the incident upon landing. By the time his flight touched down, his team at CrowdStrike had pinpointed the server used by the attacker, recovered records of their activity, and even identified a suspect. The alleged hacker had inadvertently left personal information behind while using AI tools to conduct the attacks. The incident, which CrowdStrike subsequently investigated , involved Artex, an open-source AI-powered penetration-testing tool, alongside LLMs from a variety of providers. The scale and speed of the attack illustrate why artificial intelligence has fueled growing fears about the future of cybersecurity. But Meyers isn’t panicking. “I thrive on chaos,” he says. And in a conversation with Fast Company at the company’s Fal.Con conference in Barcelona, he argues that much of the alarm surrounding AI-powered hacking is misplaced. “Fundamentally, this is nothing new. It’s just speed and volume,” he says. “AI hasn’t come up with new exploit paths or new vulnerability classes, right? It’s all the same stuff we’re already aware of.” That doesn’t mean the technology is harmless. But Meyers believes the cybersecurity industry risks confusing the capabilities of increasingly sophisticated AI models with the actual threat they pose to organizations. He’s not alone. Ciaran Martin, the former head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre, argues that much of the discussion around AI-enabled hacking has become detached from the realities of cybercrime. “To some extent, we’ve lost our mind in 2026 because of the extent of the capabilities,” he says. Martin believes companies developing frontier AI models have focused heavily on what their systems can theoretically accomplish without paying enough attention to the motivations and constraints of actual attackers. “They don’t understand threat actors. They don’t understand hackers. They don’t understand the economics and the sociology and the politics of hacking,” he says. The result, Martin suggests, is an industry increasingly alarmed by suspicious activity, even as the growing volume of automated attacks doesn’t necessarily translate into more successful compromises. That disconnect is putting pressure on security teams, which must sift through an ever-growing number of potential threats. Eerke Boiten, a cybersecurity professor at De Montfort University in the U.K., sees a similar challenge. AI is accelerating the discovery of vulnerabilities, he explains, but the ability to exploit them isn’t necessarily advancing at the same pace. That leaves already overwhelmed security teams struggling to determine which threats warrant their attention. There is, however, a potential upside: The same AI capabilities that help attackers identify vulnerabilities could also help defenders fix them and assess how difficult they are to exploit. When every vulnerability becomes an emergency For Meyers, the challenge underscores a long-standing problem with how organizations assess cybersecurity risks. He argues that the industry has become too reliant on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, or CVSS, which assigns numerical scores to security flaws on a scale of one to 10. PHP2Shell, a pair of vulnerabilities in the widely used PHP programming language that drew widespread attention, each received a score of 9.2. Meyers says CrowdStrike examined the issue before its public disclosure and concluded that exploiting the vulnerabilities would be far from straightforward. articles.title: MBZUAI’s IFM Releases PAN 2, an Open 29B World Model for Physical AI
articles.content:
The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at MBZUAI released PAN 2 , an open world model for physical intelligence. The PAN 2 world model takes a scene and a text action and simulates the outcome as video. IFM announced it on X on November 10, 2026. Weights, training code and inference code ship under Apache 2.0 . For robotics and agent developers, the pitch is simple: test a plan in simulation before acting on it. TL;DR Size: 29B-parameter diffusion transformer (MMDiT), dense. Inputs: text plus an optional first frame. Output: 704×1248 video at 24 fps, up to 20 s. Runs on: Data-center GPUs. Each worker holds the full 29B model in BF16, with block offloading as fallback. Performance: Leads 6 tested models on full plans. Trails MiniMax-H3 on single actions and human preference. Best: 34.0% full-plan completion on 100 multi-step tasks, the highest of all models tested (self-reported). Worst: About 2 in 3 plans miss a step. Physics-IQ system default: 37.48 vs 42.91 for MiniMax-H3. Bottom line: Best: a fully open world model that leads on multi-step plans. Worst: long plans still fail often, and hardware needs are high. What is PAN 2? PAN 2 is a general-purpose world model from IFM that simulates how a scene changes after an action. It follows the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture from IFM’s Critique of World Models paper. It succeeds PAN , released in November 2025. The goal is simulative reasoning . An agent proposes plans, PAN 2 simulates each one, and the agent acts on the best. How does PAN 2 work? PAN 2 splits simulation into 2 kinds of reasoning : Conceptual reasoning : An LLM reads the observation and the requested actions. It writes the next world state as structured JSON: events, timed actions bound to actors, and camera motion. Any instruction-following LLM can fill this role. IFM’s report uses Kimi K3 by default. Perceptual reasoning : A 29B MMDiT predicts the video latents. IFM trained it from scratch on hundreds of millions of annotated videos. A frozen Qwen3.5-9B text encoder conditions it. The Wan 2.2 VAE decoder renders the final frames. IFM’s ablation shows the LLM matters. With no conceptual reasoning, full-plan completion drops from 34.0% to 0.0%. Step completion falls from 75.1% to 8.7%. A format-only rewrite recovers part of the gap, reaching 27.8% full-plan completion. IFM also dropped gameplay, animation and simulation footage after early training. A 9B test model trained without it won 58% of blinded votes. Prev Click any step to jump

articles.title: US and Rest of World Must Follow China's Lead On Green Energy, Says John Kerry
articles.content: Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe -- including the US -- must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year's climate summit. As Cop31 opens -- this year the climate conference is in Turkey -- there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest "five-year plan" adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to "actively participate in and lead global climate governance". Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do. In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220 billion, and they should grow again this year; the world's largest emitter is now the world's leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there. Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south. "The only country that has hugely accelerated is China," said Kerry. "The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day." "[China] realized suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they're moving independently. There's been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump." For autocratic states without free and fair elections, seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added. "They'll see where the market is going, and they will recognize where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal," Kerry said. "Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels." He added: "The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they're going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That's the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: New malware doesn’t call home, it turns your Exchange server into its home
articles.content: There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders. A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage. The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks. While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies , enterprises should still be concerned. “Tradecraft like this tends not to stay with its inventors,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, citing a baseball analogy: “Criminal groups study nation-state techniques the way minor leaguers study a big league pitcher’s grip. What works in the majors eventually shows up in every ballpark.” Sophisticated tradecraft ESET describes Cereal as a malware toolkit that runs on Microsoft Exchange servers, receives commands and executes them in memory, maps the victim organization, and collects selected email messages. No external network infrastructure was identified; instead, the toolkit contains a passive backdoor that runs on targeted servers and provides access. It leaves little on disk. The researchers noted that one of the most interesting aspects of the toolkit is what they did not find: External C&C infrastructure. The victim’s compromised Exchange server is effectively “co-opted” to play the part. Operators send commands as separate, but similarly-structured, executables, suggesting an automated framework. An automated email collection module is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes, allowing threat actors to access and manipulate the email transport pipeline, the researchers explained. “This requires deep understanding of the inner workings of Microsoft Exchange and is a novel technique,” they wrote. They described a typical attack chain this way: An official in a national government office sends an email to a colleague at a transnational military alliance. The message goes out through a Microsoft Exchange server, just as it should; nothing looks suspicious. But before the email departs, a piece of code quietly examines it, identifies whether it is interesting, and if it is, sets aside a copy to be forwarded to “prying eyes.” The original email continues on its way as usual. The toolset demonstrated that Exchange servers are not just mail servers, they are “durable collection points,” internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft, the researchers noted. The transport pipeline reflects a level of investment in this type of technique that is “uncommon even among sophisticated APT [advanced persistent threat] actors,” they said. The researchers discovered that the malware has so far been used to target Kazakhstan and Romania. ESET attributes the toolkit to Russia-aligned APT group Turla. Attackers made a significant effort to remain undetected Experts agreed that some of the most notable aspects of Cereal are the lack of a C2 channel and the effort the attackers made to stay in stealth mode. “ESET found no attacker-controlled server. None,” Dickson noted. The victim’s own Exchange server is the command center, and the backdoor waits for encrypted requests on web paths that look like ordinary Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover, and ActiveSync traffic. “Cereal never calls home. It is home,” he said. This is dangerous because most network defenses watch for traffic leaving for a suspicious destination. But here, there is no destination to block and no server to take down. “The attackers walk in through the front door, dressed as Outlook,” he noted. Then there is the mail hook: Legitimate transport agents in Exchange allow software to inspect mail as it flows. But Cereal injects itself…

articles.title: Fish Audio Releases Live 3, a Full-Duplex Voice Model That Reacts in 186 ms
articles.content: Fish Audio has released Live 3 , a full-duplex voice model built for real-time voice agents. The Fish Audio Live 3 full-duplex voice model keeps listening while it speaks. That lets a caller pause, say “mm-hmm,” or change their mind without breaking the call. For developers, the pitch is simple. Turn-taking moves out of hand-tuned pipeline rules and into the speech model. TL;DR Product: A full-duplex voice model built for real-time voice agents Runs on: Hosted Fish Agent Platform and Fish Audio API; on-premises for enterprises. Performance: Fish Audio shows behavior demos, but publishes no benchmark scores. Best: Can decide to respond in as little as 186 ms for short reactions like “mm-hmm.” What is Fish Audio Live 3? Live 3 is a full-duplex voice model from Fish Audio that listens and speaks at the same time. The core argument is that speed and timing are different problems. An agent can reply fast and still speak at the wrong moment. A pause after “What time do you open?” usually ends a turn. A pause in the middle of a phone number does not. How does Live 3 handle turn-taking? Most voice agents split recognition, reasoning, speech generation and turn-taking across separate pipeline stages. Fish Audio team states that Live 3 moves conversational timing into the speech model. It was trained on real human conversations to learn when to acknowledge, wait, respond or stop. They framed the old approach as piling on “more rules and more thresholds.” Fish Audio instead wants the model to learn timing from data. A separate reasoning layer still holds the agent’s instructions and tools. The Fish Audio team walks through 3 behaviors: Acknowledging without taking over. A caller reads “415… 555… 0132.” Live 3 may say “okay, 415” between chunks, then wait. Telling a backchannel from an interruption. A caller saying “yeah” lets the agent continue. “Wait, actually, I just need Thursday” makes it stop. Waiting through corrections. For “two pizzas… no, three,” Live 3 waits instead of logging the wrong order. How fast is Live 3? Fish Audio states Live 3 can decide to respond in as little as 186 ms . That figure covers short reactions such as “mm-hmm,” “okay” and quick confirmations. The full answer is prepared in parallel. This is a floor for small reactions, not time-to-first-audio for a complete reply. Fish Audio has not published a latency distribution. Third-party tracker OrcaRouter also reports no Artificial Analysis score for Live 3 as of November 11. How do developers deploy Live 3? Live 3 is available on the Fish Agent Platform , through the Fish Audio API, and on-premises for enterprises. The Agents platform is in public beta. Agents expose a REST surface under /v1/agent/* . Browser sessions run through @fishaudio/agent-client or @fishaudio/agent-react . Agents can answer phone numbers, connect over WebRTC, or sit in a website widget. The Live 3 page lists 2,000,000+ library voices, including cloned voices. A pending docs pull request shows Live 3 enabled with voice.engine: "live3" . With it on, speech recognition is fixed to fish_audio:transcribe-stream-1 . Fish Audio’s current docs say that model also classifies overlaps as interruptions or acknowledgements. How much does Live 3 cost? The Live 3 page lists $0.035 per minute , down 50% from $0.07 , until December 31, 2026. It says the plan includes Live 3. The pricing docs say the $0.07 list rate covers STT, TTS, basic LLMs, knowledge retrieval and tool calls. Phone calls add $0.01 per minute . A number costs $1.20 per month . New accounts get a $5 trial balance. How does Live 3 compare with other full-duplex voice models? articles.title: 'Apple Support Community' Permanently Closing on November 20
articles.content: Apple today announced that the long-running Apple Support Community discussion forums will be permanently closing on Friday, November 20. Effectively immediately, the Apple Support Community forums are in a read-only state, with new posts no longer being accepted. The final message posted to the site appears to have been submitted at 5:49 p.m. Pacific Time today. There is still a sign-in button, but it leads to an internal portal for Apple's corporate employees. Apple's full notice added to the site: The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site . We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products. It is the end of an era. Apple offered an online discussion forum for user-to-user technical support since 1998, when it launched the Apple Tech Exchange. The forums were renamed to Apple Discussions in 2000, and then to the Apple Support Communities in 2011, before taking on their current Apple Support Community name in 2022. Apple informed MacRumors that it decided to sunset the Apple Support Community after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs. Alternatives to the Apple Support Community include the MacRumors Forums and Reddit , and customers can continue to contact Apple Support . This article, " 'Apple Support Community' Permanently Closing on November 20 " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: M John Harrison Becomes First Sci-Fi Author To Win Booker Prize
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award's history. Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison's was "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world." She called it "a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page". Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the 50,000-pound award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening. The End of Everything, Harrison's first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. At 198 pages, it was the shortest book on the shortlist. Mary Beard, chair of the judges, said the decision was unanimous, reached after a full day of discussion. "It's a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile -- and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism," she said. "One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won't matter either This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
